posts.html:
A confession in four humiliations and one glorious moment

I.

The headmaster made the announcement during morning prayers, the way headmasters always deliver news that will change the course of someone’s life — flatly, between the attendance register and the lunch break schedule.

“There is an inter-school song competition. All interested participants must go through a screen test. If you qualify, you will represent the school.”

The words floated over the courtyard, past the serious students already calculating their chances, past the talented ones already rehearsing in their heads, and landed — somehow — in mine.

I am not entirely sure what possessed me. I had no training. No particular talent that anyone, including myself, had ever noticed. I didn’t even have a song picked out. But there has always lived inside me a creature that perks up at the word competition the way a stray dog perks up at the smell of food — not because it has a plan, but because it simply cannot help itself.

So I went.

II.

The room was full of hopefuls. I sat among them, listening to each one step up, sing their piece, and step off — and I was still thinking about what I would sing. There is a particular kind of person who decides to improvise at a singing audition. I was that person.

When they called my name, I walked to the stage with the confidence of someone who has not yet understood what is about to happen to them.

The microphone looked simple enough. I leaned into it.

It shrieked.

The teacher looked up. “Keep some distance between the microphone and your mouth.”

I nodded and stepped back. And in that single, clumsy moment — the feedback, the correction, the entire room watching — I forgot the song. Every song. Every word of every song I had ever known in my entire life simply vacated my mind like passengers abandoning a sinking ship.

I stood there. Seconds passed. The kind of seconds that feel like they’ve been specially manufactured to be longer than normal.

“You can’t stand there forever,” my teacher said, not unkindly, though it did not feel that way. “There are others waiting.”

The only thing that surfaced from the wreckage of my memory was the school prayer. Which I then sang — with, I must say, considerable soul — until the teacher raised his hand to stop me.

He was quiet for a moment. Then:

“Sa-re-ga-ma-pa-dha-ni — all coming together at the same time. Has nobody ever told you not to sing in public?” He paused for dramatic effect. “If nobody has, I am telling you now: never try singing ever. It is going to be hazardous for mankind.”

The room erupted. And I — because what else do you do when you are the punchline — laughed with them. Loudly. So they would think I was in on the joke, and not notice that some small part of me had just been quietly folded up and put away.

III.

Here is the strange thing. I never stopped.

Not on stages — I had learned my lessons about stages — but everywhere else. On window seats of buses and trains, with the landscape rolling past and nobody able to escape me. In quiet offices during slow afternoons. In rooms where people were too polite to say anything and simply pretended I wasn’t there, hoping the silence of their disapproval would extinguish me.

It never did.

I began to fancy that I sang with emotion, at least. I used to console myself with this privately: the notes may be wrong, but the feeling is right. Tolerant souls occasionally confirmed the first half of that theory. The second half, they left alone.

But the hunger — the specific, unreasonable hunger to sing on a stage, in front of real people, with a real microphone — that never went away. It just waited. The way all unreasonable hungers do.

IV. The Night of Helious

Engineering college brings with it many gifts. Freedom. Chaos. The terrifying discovery of who you actually are when nobody from your childhood is watching.

And for me — unexpectedly, beautifully — it brought Helious.

Helious was our college cultural festival. One of those annual explosions of colour, noise, terrible sound systems, and genuine joy that engineering colleges somehow produce better than anyone else. And in my final year, through a combination of persistence and the kind of enthusiastic volunteering that people mistake for competence, I found myself on the organizing committee.

I had the stage. I had the access. I had, for perhaps the first and last time in my life, control.

The poet in me had been writing in Odia for years — private lines, quiet verses that I kept mostly to myself. That year, I had set one of them to the melody of a popular Odia tune that everyone in the audience would recognize. I had been carrying this arrangement in my head for weeks, the way you carry something fragile, not quite believing it will survive the journey.

The night of the festival arrived. A thousand students filled the ground.

I walked to the microphone during a gap in the programme — calm the way only the truly deluded are calm — and I sang my poem. My words. My melody. My moment, finally, after all those years of bus windows and empty corridors and teachers telling me I was a hazard to mankind.

The stage lights were in my eyes. Bright, warm, absolute. Beyond them: darkness. A thousand people dissolved into a single, breathing shadow that I could hear but not see.

I finished.

Silence.

Not scattered applause, not the embarrassed murmuring of an audience unsure what they had witnessed. Silence. Complete and total.

Now, there are several explanations for this. The uncharitable ones involve acoustics, pitch, and the general welfare of the assembled crowd. But I prefer my own interpretation, which I have held onto carefully for many years now:

They were mesmerized.

A thousand engineers, the kinds of people trained to analyse, critique, and argue about everything — rendered speechless. By my poetry. By my voice. By the sheer unexpected audacity of a boy who had been told he was a hazard to mankind standing under the lights and singing his own words into the dark.

They simply forgot to clap.

It is, I think, the most likely explanation.

V.

Then came the colleague.

He approached me one afternoon with the careful expression of someone delivering difficult news to a child. “Sakti,” he said, “why don’t you try recording your songs? Or even — a radio station?”

Something inside me soared. I was milliseconds away from saying you know, I never had any formal training, but I always felt the music— when he finished his sentence.

“At least then I can switch off the radio.”

The room laughed. I laughed. We all laughed together, which is the great social mercy extended to those of us who are perpetually, lovably wrong about ourselves.

Coda

I still ask people, sometimes, “Don’t you feel the pain in the song when I sing?”

They always say yes. Always.

“Yes — in our ears.”

And we all laugh again.

I have been laughed at for this for more years than I care to count. I have been advised, warned, gently discouraged, loudly discouraged, and once — memorably — described as a hazard to mankind by a qualified music teacher.

The singer in me has heard all of this and found it completely irrelevant.

Because I know something most people don’t. I know what it feels like to stand under stage lights with a thousand souls in the dark in front of you, and sing your own words into that silence.

It doesn’t matter what they thought. What matters is that for one night, the stray dog had a stage.

And he sang.

— Stray Dog

posts.title: Fragment: Consume, Digest, Excrete
posts.seoTitle: Fragment: Consume, Digest, Excrete – Life as Sakti
posts.description: In biology, the cycle is simple: you consume, you digest, and you excrete. If any part of that system fails, you get sick. I’ve realized the same applies to our digital lives. For the past several months, I have been consuming at a breakneck speed. My "diet" has been a relentless stream of LinkedIn insights,…
posts.html:
In biology, the cycle is simple: you consume, you digest, and you excrete. If any part of that system fails, you get sick.

I’ve realized the same applies to our digital lives.

For the past several months, I have been consuming at a breakneck speed. My “diet” has been a relentless stream of LinkedIn insights, Medium deep-dives, X threads, and niche blogs. But without a way to process it, all that consumption resulted in a kind of “intellectual heartburn”—discomfort, confusion, and a cluttered mind.

The Digestion Phase

To settle the heartburn, I started building. Digestion, for me, is the act of turning passive consumption into active creation. I moved from being a spectator to an architect, building projects ranging from the sentimental to the ambitious:

  • A Bengali Calendar app for my mother.
  • A custom MCP to manage my social media presence.
  • Reviving my incomplete book manuscripts.
  • An AI Agent specifically for Python coding.
  • A “Deep Research & Fake Filter” to clean up my daily information intake.

This is on top of my day-to-day at Altera, where I live in GitHub Copilot. For my personal projects, I’ve moved from Claude Code to experimenting with Anti Gravity.

Building has helped. The confusion is clearing. But it has created a new problem: I am glued to my chair, day and night. I feel fragmented.

The Necessity of Excretion

This is where the third step comes in: Excretion. To maintain a healthy mental ecosystem, I have to let go. I have to purge the noise to make room for what matters.

My “Excretion Policy” moving forward:

  1. The “No” List: A strict policy on what I will not consume anymore. If it doesn’t add value to my core goals, it’s out.
  2. AI Fasting: Scheduled time where I am completely out of the loop. No models, no prompts, no screens.
  3. Tool Monogamy: I’ve decided to master one tool at a time until I’ve exhausted its utility. Jumping between every new shiny AI tool leads to a satisfied ego but a shallow understanding.
  4. Hand-Coding as Vitality: I am re-learning Python, Rust, and Go through various platforms, not just to generate code, but to understand it deeply enough to write it by hand. It’s about keeping my own cognitive “muscles” alive while the AI does the heavy lifting.

It’s been a fascinating journey so far, but the lesson is clear: If you want to stay sane in the age of AI, you cannot just consume.

Consume. Digest. Excrete. Repeat for system health.

posts.title: The Architect Who Couldn’t Manage His Own Clock
posts.seoTitle: The Architect Who Couldn’t Manage His Own Clock – Life as Sakti
posts.description: How an AI reading loop forced me to finally bring my house — my mind — in order Act I — The Loop That Wouldn't Stop It started, like most dangerous things in my life, with a good idea. I had built a reading loop — AI-assisted, naturally. Every morning I would feed articles into…
posts.html:
How an AI reading loop forced me to finally bring my house — my mind — in order

Act I — The Loop That Wouldn’t Stop

It started, like most dangerous things in my life, with a good idea.

I had built a reading loop — AI-assisted, naturally. Every morning I would feed articles into Claude, ask it to summarise, extract insights, and suggest what I should write next. Then I’d draft a piece. Claude would refine it. I’d publish. The loop was elegant. The loop was productive. The loop was, I told myself, the future of knowledge work.

What I didn’t notice — not for the first few weeks, anyway — was that the loop had a flaw baked into its very elegance.

I was reading more than ever. Writing more than ever. But I had quietly stopped finishing things. A Medium draft sat at 80% for eleven days. A GitHub repo that needed three more commits gathered dust. An email to my cross-geo team about the upcoming PI planning sat as a red unread reminder in my own inbox.

I had optimised the intake. I had forgotten to optimise the output.

That sentence — scribbled in the margin of a notebook while waiting for a CI pipeline to finish — became the pivot point of everything that followed.

Act II — The Cheatsheet on the Wall

A colleague shared Dr. Miro Bada’s infographic: How to Master Time Management — The Cheatsheet to Win Back Your Time. Fifteen frameworks on a single page. I had seen most of them before, scattered across blog posts and productivity books. But seeing them all together, in one visual, did something different to my brain.

It felt like walking into a cluttered room and suddenly having someone turn on all the lights at once.

I printed it. I stuck it on the wall beside my monitor. And for the first time in weeks, I stopped reading and started looking — really looking — at how I was spending my hours.

Here is what I found, and here is what I did about it.

Act III — Fifteen Mirrors, One Reflection

1. The Domino Effect — Stop Starting, Start Sequencing

My calendar was a museum of parallel beginnings. Three architectural documents in draft. Two LinkedIn posts half-written. One book chapter stalled at a metaphor I couldn’t crack.

The Domino Effect asks a simple question: which task, when completed, makes the next one easier? I restructured my week around this logic. The PI planning summary first — because it unblocked five team leads. The Medium article second — because finishing it cleared the mental noise. The GitHub commits third — because they were small and fast, the kind of domino that falls in ten minutes and makes you feel human again.

2. The 1-3-5 Rule — The Morning Contract

I began writing a daily contract with myself. One big thing. Three medium things. Five small things. Not a wishlist — a contract. The difference is accountability.

The AI loop actually helps here: I now ask Claude each morning to help me triage the day’s tasks into this structure. It takes four minutes. It saves two hours of drift.

3. The Not-Todo List — The Art of Strategic Abandonment

This one stung.

I identified six recurring tasks that I was doing out of habit, not value. Three I automated. Two I delegated to team members who were frankly better at them than I was. One I simply eliminated — a weekly report nobody was reading.

Freedom, it turns out, is sometimes just a deleted calendar invite.

4. Airplane Mode — The Sacred Window

Between 6:30 AM and 8:00 AM, my phone goes into airplane mode. No Slack. No email. No news. This is when I read, write, and think. The AI loop now lives entirely in this window. Claude gets my full attention. In return, I get my full morning.

5. The 5-Second Rule — Launching Into the Uncomfortable

5-4-3-2-1. Launch.

I use this specifically for the tasks I have been avoiding — the difficult feedback email, the architectural decision document that required me to admit I had been wrong about something for three months. The countdown is ridiculous. It works anyway.

6. S.M.A.R.T Goals — Making the Fuzzy Concrete

My AI reading loop was not SMART. It had no defined endpoint, no measurable output, no time boundary. I added one rule: every reading session must produce one publishable insight within 48 hours. Suddenly, the loop had a shape.

7. The Seesaw System — Balancing the High and the Low

Architecture reviews and PI planning are cognitively heavy. Reviewing pull requests and updating documentation are lighter. I now interleave them deliberately — heavy task, light task, heavy task, light task. My energy curve stopped looking like a cliff and started looking like a wave.

8. The 80/20 Rule — Finding the Vital Few

Twenty percent of my tasks drive eighty percent of my professional impact. For me, that twenty percent is: strategic documents, key stakeholder communications, and the Medium articles that shape my thought leadership positioning.

I put those tasks in the morning. Everything else gets the afternoon.

9. Task Batching — The Context-Switch Tax

Every time you switch contexts, you pay a tax. I was paying it dozens of times a day. Now I batch: all code reviews in one block, all writing in one block, all meetings compressed into Tuesday and Thursday afternoons. The rest of the week breathes.

10. Eat Your Frog — The Hardest Thing First

My frog changes daily. Some days it is a difficult conversation. Some days it is a blank document that needs 800 words I do not yet have. Some days it is simply getting out of bed early enough to have a morning at all.

I eat it first. Always. The rest of the day tastes better for it.

11. The Eisenhower Matrix — Triage as a Discipline

I built a simple habit: every Sunday evening, I run the week’s tasks through the matrix. Urgent + Important gets my mornings. Important + Not Urgent gets scheduled. Urgent + Not Important gets delegated. Not Important + Not Urgent gets deleted without guilt.

The matrix does not give you more time. It gives you better decisions about the time you have.

12. The Unfinished Symphony — The Power of Beginning

I had always been afraid to start things I could not finish in one sitting. The Unfinished Symphony principle inverted this. Now I deliberately start things — a paragraph, a diagram, a code stub — knowing I will not finish them today. The brain, it turns out, does not like loose ends. It works on them in the background, whether you ask it to or not.

Several of my best Medium paragraphs were written in the shower, solving a problem I started the night before.

13. The Pomodoro Technique — Time as Ritual

25 minutes. 5-minute break. Repeat. I pair this with the Airplane Mode window for deep work. What I discovered: the technique is not really about time. It is about permission — permission to stop, permission to rest, permission to begin again.

14. Time Blocking — Designing the Day

My calendar now has three types of blocks: Deep Work (marked in blue, non-negotiable), Collaborative Work (meetings, reviews, team calls), and Recovery (lunch, walk, nothing-in-particular). The third category was the hardest to add. It was the most important.

15. Power Hour + Closing the Day — The Bookends

I begin with a Power Hour: one uninterrupted hour on the week’s most important project. I end with a Closing ritual: wrap up open loops, review what I completed, write three priorities for tomorrow.

The closing ritual, specifically, changed how I sleep. The open loops were not keeping me awake — I had just never given myself a formal place to put them down.

Act IV — What the AI Loop Looks Like Now

The loop did not disappear. It matured.

I still use Claude every morning. I still read, synthesise, and write. But now the loop has a container: it lives in the Airplane Mode window, structured by the 1-3-5 rule, launched by the 5-Second Rule, and bounded by a Power Hour timer. The Eisenhower Matrix decides whether a new reading topic earns a slot in my week. The Domino Effect decides the sequence.

The result: I publish more, drift less, and finish what I start.

The frameworks in Dr. Bada’s cheatsheet are not new ideas. Most of them are decades old. What is new — what I believe is the essential skill for anyone building in the age of AI — is the discipline to apply them when the tools around you are actively rewarding distraction with the illusion of productivity.

Reading faster is not the same as thinking better.

Writing more is not the same as writing well.

A loop that generates output is not the same as a mind that has direction.

Coda — Bringing the House in Order

The Bhagavad Gita speaks of chitta-shuddhi — the purification of the mind, the clearing of the inner house before any great work can be done. I am not a philosopher. I am an engineering manager with a backlog and a calendar and a persistent sense that there is more I could be doing with the hours I have.

But I have come to believe that the frameworks above are a modern chitta-shuddhi. They are not productivity tricks. They are acts of respect — for your own attention, for your team’s time, for the work that deserves to be done well.

The AI will keep reading. The AI will keep writing. The AI will keep suggesting what comes next.

But the architect of that loop — the one who decides what gets built, and when, and why — that has to be you.

Bring your house in order. Then build.

posts.title: The Morning Before the World Woke Up
posts.seoTitle: The Morning Before the World Woke Up – Life as Sakti
posts.description: How One Page a Day from India's Ancient Wisdom Traditions Can Change Everything A woman captures a quiet moment of reading as the sun rises over a misty mountain range. It was 4:47 AM when I first read the line that broke me open. Not "broke" in the dramatic sense. Broke like a seed breaks…
posts.html:
How One Page a Day from India’s Ancient Wisdom Traditions Can Change Everything

It was 4:47 AM when I first read the line that broke me open.

Not “broke” in the dramatic sense. Broke like a seed breaks — that quiet, underground rupture before something green pushes through.

The verse was from the Bhagavad Gita. Just one. I hadn’t planned to change my life that morning. I had only planned to wake up before the noise started.

A Book a Day Was a Lie I Told Myself

We’ve all been there. The bookshelf that doubles as a monument to good intentions. The highlighted pages we’ll “go back to.” The productivity guru who swears by reading 52 books a year.

I tried. I failed. And somewhere between trying and failing, I missed the entire point.

The ancient traditions of India never asked you to consume wisdom. They asked you to sit with it. To let it breathe inside you. To carry it like a lamp into the ordinary Tuesday of your life.

Ryan Holiday built an empire of morning rituals around Stoic philosophy — one quote, one reflection, one journal entry. The remarkable thing is, he was doing what the Guru Granth Sahib already knew. What the Dhammapada already knew. What the rishis sitting in forest hermitages thousands of years ago already practiced.

They called it Svadhyaya — self-study through sacred reading.

One page was always enough.

The Story of the River and the Stone

There is an old image that returns to me often: water doesn’t break stone through force. It breaks stone through return. The same gentle pressure, again and again, over time, until the hardest surface yields.

A page a day is not about information. It is about return.

You return to the Yoga Vasistha and its wild, luminous claim that the world you perceive is a dream the mind is having. You return to Rumi’s Masnavi — not to understand it, but to be confused by it in a slightly different way than yesterday. You return to the Japji Sahib, whose opening line asks a question so large it takes a lifetime to hear: How do we become truthful before the One who is Truth itself?

Each morning, you return. And slowly — imperceptibly, like a stone beside a river — you change.

The Texts That Were Always Designed for This

Here is what most people don’t realize: India’s greatest philosophical texts were never meant to be read cover to cover in an airport lounge.

The Dhammapada is 423 verses. The Buddha’s distilled teaching on how to live. Two verses a morning and you’ve spent a year walking beside the most awake mind in human history.

The Upanishads — those radical, dazzling inquiries into the nature of consciousness — were oral traditions passed from teacher to student one insight at a time. Eknath Easwaran, one of their most beloved translators, structured his commentary explicitly as daily readings. He understood the original architecture.

The Yoga Vasistha Sara, the distilled essence of one of India’s longest philosophical epics, fits in your palm. A paragraph before breakfast, and you are suddenly wondering what the word “I” actually refers to. Good. That is the point.

The Masnavi of Rumi — Sufi wisdom in the form of story, metaphor, and poetry — rewards slowness. One story, one couplet. Let it echo through your afternoon.

The Japji Sahib from the Guru Granth Sahib was not written to be finished. It was written to be lived. It is the first prayer of the Sikh day, recited by millions each dawn, its cadences worn smooth by generations of devoted return.

These are not books. They are companions.

The Ritual (And Why It Has to Be Small)

The enemy of transformation is ambition.

We set the alarm for 5 AM, pull out the leather-bound journal, light the lap, and commit to an hour of morning philosophy. It works for nine days. Then life happens. Then we feel like failures. Then the book goes back on the shelf.

The tradition asks for something far less heroic, and far more powerful.

One page. One verse. One story.

Here is the practice, stripped to its bones:

Before your phone tells you what to think, before the inbox makes its demands, before the world inserts its agenda into your morning — open the text. Read one page. Not two. One.

Then close the book. Sit for a moment. Ask yourself: What does this have to do with what I’m walking into today?

Write the answer down. Even three sentences. Even one.

That’s it.

You’ve just done something the Vedic tradition considers sacred. You’ve practiced Svadhyaya. You’ve watered the inner life before the outer one makes its noise.

What Changes (And When)

Nothing changes at first. This is important to know.

Week one, you feel slightly philosophical and mildly self-congratulatory. Week two, you miss two days and feel guilty. Week three, something shifts. You’re in a difficult meeting and a line from the Gita surfaces — “You have a right to perform your prescribed duties, but you are not entitled to the fruits of your actions” — and instead of tightening with anxiety, you feel something release.

That’s when you understand what the tradition was trying to give you all along.

Not information. Equanimity. Not knowledge. A way to stand inside your own life without being consumed by it.

By month three, the practice has become structural — like brushing your teeth, but for the part of you that asks why am I doing any of this?

Which Text Do You Choose?

Start with one. Just one. For a year.

If you are drawn to the question of action — what it means to do your duty without attachment to outcomes — begin with the Bhagavad Gita. There are beautiful daily-reading editions organized by Ravi Ravindra and others, 700 verses mapped to 365 mornings.

If you are drawn to the question of consciousness — what the mind is, what “I” is, whether the dreamer and the dream are different — enter the Upanishads through Easwaran’s patient, brilliant commentary.

If you are drawn to the question of suffering and release — how to live with loss, with change, with the impossibility of holding anything — sit each morning with the Dhammapada.

If you are drawn to the heart, the longing, the ache of something vast inside a small life — let Rumi’s Masnavi be your companion.

If you want a daily practice that has been tested by millions of lives across five centuries — begin the Japji Sahib. Let its rhythm become the rhythm of your mornings.

A Word About What This Is Not

This is not about becoming spiritual in a way that floats above ordinary life.

The Gita was spoken on a battlefield. The Dhammapada was offered to people struggling with jealousy, grief, and fear. The Masnavi is full of imperfect, stumbling human beings finding grace in the most ridiculous circumstances.

This is a practice for the person who has a 9 AM standup. For the person who is navigating a difficult manager, a difficult relationship, a difficult self. For the senior leader who has every credential and still wonders, in the quiet moments, if they are building something that matters.

One page a day is not an escape from that life. It is the practice of meeting it with a little more of yourself intact.

The Morning Ritual, Reclaimed

Somewhere in Bengaluru, or Chennai, or any city where the traffic starts early and the day hits hard — a morning is happening right now where someone woke up before the noise began.

They made chai. They sat near the window. They opened a worn copy of the Dhammapada, or the Yoga Vasistha Sara, or the Guru Granth Sahib. They read one page.

They are not a saint. They are not a philosopher. They are just someone who decided, quietly, that the inner life deserved five minutes before the outer one claimed the rest.

And day by day — like water on stone, like a seed breaking underground — they are becoming someone slightly more awake than before.

One page was enough.

It always was.

The texts mentioned in this piece — the Bhagavad Gita, Upanishads, Yoga Vasistha Sara, Dhammapada, Masnavi, Conference of the Birds, Tattvartha Sutra, and Japji Sahib — are among the most profound works in human history. Each tradition has its own commentary lineage; seek out translators like Eknath Easwaran, Ravi Ravindra, and Jawid Mojaddedi for accessible, scholarly, and deeply human entry points.

If this resonated, I write regularly about leadership, technology, and the examined life. Connect with me on LinkedIn or explore more at saktibagchi.in.

posts.title: Experience Changes How You Prompt
posts.seoTitle: Experience Changes How You Prompt – Life as Sakti
posts.description: Unlocking the Power of Experience: How Prompting in AI Can Elevate Your Knowledge! A seasoned professional demonstrates advanced AI-assisted workflows in a modern office environment. A junior developer sees AI as a shortcut. I see it as a collaborator. Here is why experience changes everything about how you prompt. In my first job in Bangalore…
posts.html:
Unlocking the Power of Experience: How Prompting in AI Can Elevate Your Knowledge!

A junior developer sees AI as a shortcut. I see it as a collaborator. Here is why experience changes everything about how you prompt.

In my first job in Bangalore in 2000, I was a software engineer trainee with a simple belief: if I could think logically, step by step, everything would fall into place.

Then I met my first real blocker.

My manager would not let me send emails.

Not “try harder” or “be careful”. Literally: no emails to our US counterparts. No code check-ins. No commits. And I was furious.

I remember thinking: This is exactly why people say managers are bad.

But the reality was more nuanced, and it taught me the most enduring lesson of my career.

The two-hour email

Our US counterparts sat in Tucson, Arizona. The overlap window was small.

If we asked the wrong question, or communicated poorly, the cost was not “some back-and-forth”. The cost was a full day.

So my manager would do something that felt ridiculous at the time.

They made me sit next to them for up to two hours, rewriting a single email.

First question:

“What do you want as a response?”

My answer was always some version of:

“I want them to either approve the design or tell me if I am fundamentally wrong.”

Then the editing began.

They would reorder sentences.

They would delete a line I felt was “important”.

They would highlight one sentence and say, “This is the only thing they need to respond to.”

By the time we hit send, my original email barely existed.

At first, I read it as power.

Later, I saw it as craft.

Because the responses we got back were exactly what we needed. Approval. Or a clear correction. In minutes. Inside that thin overlap window.

That email saved days.

And eventually, after about a year of this, my manager let me write and send emails on my own.

The surprising part is: I have been using that same mental model ever since.

A concrete AI example: two prompts, two different worlds

Fast-forward to today.

A junior developer on a team will often treat AI like a vending machine.

They type something like:

“Can you write a design for this feature?”

They get something clean, confident, and… generic.

It sounds correct because it is written well. But it does not engage with the real risks.

It does not ask the hard questions.

It does not reveal what it does not know.

Now here is the “experienced” version of the same task.

Instead of asking for “a design”, I ask the AI to play the role I need, with the constraints I actually have.

“You are a senior engineer reviewing a design proposal. Context: we have only a 30–60 minute overlap with the US team, so we need to minimize back-and-forth. Goal: produce a one-page design email that gets an approval or a specific correction in one reply.

Feature: [brief description].

Constraints: [existing system, latency, data model, whatever is real].

Please:

  1. Ask the 5 most important clarifying questions first.
  1. Then draft the email in a format that makes it easy to approve.
  1. Include a short “what could go wrong” section with 3–5 risks.”

The difference is not the model.

The difference is that the second prompt contains:

  • Context
  • A clear outcome
  • A defined role
  • Constraints
  • A response format
  • And most importantly: a sensitivity to the cost of a bad response

The real insight: prompting well requires knowing what “bad” looks like

A junior developer can be smart and hardworking and still struggle to prompt well.

Not because they lack vocabulary.

Because prompting is not just about asking.

It is about recognizing.

Recognizing when an answer is:

  • technically plausible but operationally impossible
  • correct in theory but risky in practice
  • missing the one question that will block the project later
  • confidently vague

That recognition takes time.

It comes from getting burned by ambiguity.

It comes from sending the wrong email and losing a day.

It comes from seeing a project drift because nobody forced clarity at the start.

In other words:

Prompting well requires knowing what a bad answer looks like.

And that knowledge takes years.

Why I no longer see AI as a shortcut

AI is powerful, but it is not magic.

If you treat it like a shortcut, you will mostly get shortcuts back.

If you treat it like a collaborator, you will start doing what good collaborators do:

  • you give context
  • you align on outcomes
  • you define constraints
  • you ask for the response format you need
  • you iterate with intention

That is not “prompt engineering”.

That is simply communication.

It is the same lesson my manager taught me, one two-hour email at a time.

One question to close

What has your experience taught AI that a textbook could not?

posts.title: Drowning in Abundance: My Life at the Edge of the AI Age
posts.seoTitle: Drowning in Abundance: My Life at the Edge of the AI Age – Life as Sakti
posts.description: For the past several months, I have been reading, practicing, and writing about AI — obsessively, almost embarrassingly. And then Claude and OpenAI dropped their latest releases. Claude Cowork arrived. And something shifted. Earlier, my head was a crowded marketplace of ideas with almost no hands to execute them. Now, the hands are faster than…
posts.html:
For the past several months, I have been reading, practicing, and writing about AI — obsessively, almost embarrassingly. And then Claude and OpenAI dropped their latest releases. Claude Cowork arrived. And something shifted.

Earlier, my head was a crowded marketplace of ideas with almost no hands to execute them. Now, the hands are faster than the ideas. That is a strange and wonderful problem to have.

Here is the first sign I noticed something had fundamentally changed in me: I stopped hitting my daily limits on Instagram and YouTube.

For nearly a year, I had set a strict 30-minute cap on both — a small act of sanity in a noisy world. I held that boundary like a promise to myself. But in the past few days, I haven’t even come close to the limit. Not because I am suppressing the urge. Simply because I don’t feel the pull anymore. Practicing, reading, and writing about AI has quietly replaced the scroll.

I got busier. But it’s a different kind of busy.

You know that feeling when you plan a vacation hoping to do absolutely nothing — to just lie on a beach, stare at the sky, let your mind go blank? And then you find yourself hiking at 6 AM, exploring every corner of the city, physically exhausted but oddly alive?

That’s exactly what AI is doing to my calendar.

It was supposed to free up time. And it does — in pockets. But those pockets don’t stay empty for long. They fill up with new experiments, new projects, new questions. Every block of freed time becomes a canvas. The abundance is almost overwhelming.

It feels like a jumbo buffet opening its doors to someone who hasn’t eaten in days. You don’t slow down. You load the plate.

Last week, I turned that energy toward my WordPress website.

I used to spend hours — sometimes entire evenings — editing layouts, customizing pages, wrestling with plugins. It was a labor of love, but labor nonetheless. This time, with AI as my co-pilot, I transformed the pages in minutes.

And then I sat back and asked myself a question that felt slightly absurd given where I was writing it: Do I even need WordPress anymore?

Yes, I realize the irony. Writing a “why I might leave WordPress” post on WordPress. The universe has a sense of humor.

But here is the truth: if I have a domain, I can build pages and host them. It’s not as plug-and-play as WordPress, but with a little discipline and curiosity — both of which seem to be in good supply these days — it is entirely possible. The gatekeeping is gone.

I also built an MCP — a small but satisfying project — that takes a finished blog post and generates shareable content for LinkedIn, Facebook, Twitter, and WhatsApp in one go. My social media posting time is now close to zero.

The tools are falling into place. The workflow is tightening.

But here is what I have realized stays irreplaceable in all of this: original thought.

AI can amplify an idea. It can execute, refine, and distribute it at speed. But the spark — the original observation, the genuine insight, the lived experience — that still has to come from somewhere human. From somewhere inside.

So I am carving out 2.5 hours every day just to read.

Not online articles. Not newsletters. Books. Physical, distraction-free, margin-scribbling books. Because that is where I find the quiet necessary for real absorption. That is where original ideas still have room to breathe.

I am sharing this not as a productivity prescription, but simply as a snapshot of one person’s state of mind in the middle of a strange and exciting moment in history.

If any of this resonates with you — if you too are standing at this same buffet, plate in hand, slightly overwhelmed but smiling — let’s give each other a quiet thumbs up.

We are figuring this out together.

posts.title: From Confused to Confident: The AI Glossary Nobody Asked For (But Everyone Needs)
posts.seoTitle: From Confused to Confident: The AI Glossary Nobody Asked For (But Everyone Needs) – Life as Sakti
posts.description: Imagine you just walked into a casual discussion with colleagues or friends. Everyone around you is throwing around words like RAG, MCP, Agentic AI, LLM. You smile and nod. Inside, you're thinking: "Did I miss a memo?" You didn't. The world just moved fast. Let me slow it down. Grab a cup of chai. I'll…
posts.html:
Imagine you just walked into a casual discussion with colleagues or friends. Everyone around you is throwing around words like RAG, MCP, Agentic AI, LLM. You smile and nod. Inside, you’re thinking: “Did I miss a memo?”

You didn’t. The world just moved fast. Let me slow it down.

Grab a cup of chai. I’ll tell you a story.

The Library and the Librarian — Understanding LLM

Picture the largest library ever built. Not just the Library of Congress or British Library or the National Library — imagine a library that swallowed the entire internet. Every book, every blog, every Wikipedia article, every Reddit argument at 2 AM. All of it, shelved and catalogued.

Now imagine a librarian who grew up inside that library. From childhood to adulthood, this librarian read everything. Every page. Every footnote. They didn’t memorize it word for word, but they absorbed the patterns. They know how sentences flow. They know that when someone says “I’m feeling blue,” they don’t mean they consumed poison.

That librarian is your Large Language Model — LLM.

When you type a question, you’re not searching a database. You’re having a conversation with someone who has read more than any human ever could. GPT, Claude, Gemini — these are all LLMs. Different librarians, same basic story.

But here’s the catch. The librarian stopped reading on a specific date. Everything after that? They don’t know. Ask them about yesterday’s news, and they’ll look at you blankly.

Which brings us to our next character.

The Librarian Gets a Research Assistant — Understanding RAG

Our brilliant librarian has a gap. They’re stuck in the past. So we hire them a research assistant.

Every time you ask a question, before the librarian answers, the research assistant runs to the current shelves — your company documents, today’s news, last week’s reports, your product manuals — pulls out the most relevant pages, and slides them across the desk.

The librarian reads those fresh pages and then answers you. Not from old memory alone, but from memory plus current context.

This is RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation.

The “retrieval” part is the research assistant running to fetch relevant documents. The “generation” part is the librarian crafting a beautiful, coherent answer from what they know and what they just read.

This is why AI can now answer questions about your company’s specific policies, your patient records, your internal knowledge base — without having been trained on any of it.

Smart librarian. Faster research assistant. Better answers.

Teaching the Librarian to Use a Telephone — Understanding MCP

Now our librarian is wise and well-read. But they’re still stuck inside the library. They can’t do anything outside it. They can’t check the weather. They can’t look up your calendar. They can’t send an email.

So we give them a telephone directory. A special one.

This directory lists all the tools and services in the world — Google Calendar, your hospital’s database, a weather API, a ticketing system — and most importantly, it tells the librarian exactly how to call each one. The format to use. The words to speak. The protocol to follow.

This telephone directory is MCP — Model Context Protocol.

It’s not magic. It’s a standard. Like how every electrical outlet in India follows a standard so any plug fits. MCP creates a universal language so AI can plug into any tool, any system, any service — without custom wiring every single time.

When you hear someone say “Claude can now connect to your Slack” or “the AI can read your Google Drive” — MCP is often the handshake making that happen behind the scenes.

The Librarian Who Takes Initiative — Understanding Agentic AI

Until now, our librarian waited. You asked, they answered. A very polite, reactive arrangement.

But what if you walked in one morning and said: “Plan my entire product launch for next quarter” — and then left for coffee?

An Agentic AI doesn’t wait for your next instruction at every step. It breaks down the big goal into smaller tasks, figures out what to do first, uses its tools, checks the result, adjusts, and keeps going — until the job is done or it hits a wall it can’t climb alone.

Think of it like the difference between a junior employee who needs a checklist for every hour versus a senior manager who you brief once and then they run with it.

“Agentic” simply means acting with agency — with the ability to plan, decide, and execute with some level of autonomy.

This is exciting. And yes, a little bit terrifying. Which is exactly why we have guardrails, oversight, and a lot of very nervous engineers watching dashboards.

The Whole Team Working Together — Understanding AI Agents

Now imagine you have not just one librarian-manager, but a team.

One agent specializes in research. One handles scheduling. One writes code. One reviews it. One manages customer emails. Each one is an AI built for a specific job, armed with specific tools, talking to each other through defined protocols.

Welcome to AI Agents — or more precisely, Multi-Agent Systems.

An AI Agent is an LLM with a role, tools, memory, and a goal. Give it a name, give it a purpose, connect it to the right data and systems, and it becomes your autonomous digital colleague.

When a hospital says “our AI agent pre-authorizes insurance claims overnight” — that’s an agent. When a software company says “our agent reviews pull requests and suggests fixes” — that’s an agent. When a bank says “our agent detects fraud in real-time” — that’s an agent.

Agents are the LLM’s grown-up, working-world version.

Putting It All Together

Let me draw the picture one final time, simply:

LLM is the brain — trained on massive data, generates intelligent responses.

RAG gives that brain fresh, relevant documents to work from — so it’s never outdated.

MCP gives that brain hands — the ability to connect with tools, systems, and the real world.

Agentic AI gives that brain initiative — it plans and acts, not just responds.

AI Agents put that brain to work — specialized, autonomous, collaborative digital workers.

Why This Matters to You

Whether you’re a doctor, an engineer, a manager, or an entrepreneur — these are not future technologies. They are here. They are reshaping how hospitals run, how software gets built, how businesses make decisions.

You don’t need to build them. But understanding what they are — just well enough to ask the right questions, challenge the right assumptions, and make informed decisions — that’s the new professional literacy.

The discussion is in full swing. Now you know what everyone’s talking about.

Go join the conversation.

Here is a pictorial format as ready reference.

If this article made at least one concept click for you, share it with someone who’s still nodding and smiling at parties. They’ll thank you.

posts.title: Fragment 2 – Defragmenting My Mind
posts.seoTitle: Fragment 2 – Defragmenting My Mind – Life as Sakti
posts.description: This is second in my fragment series where I share what all running in my life and mind. I do it for my own brain defragmentation. A week that was nothing less than a roller-coaster ride. The highs were creating my first agent, completing a 40-hour fast, and getting better at Python. The lows were…
posts.html:
This is second in my fragment series where I share what all running in my life and mind. I do it for my own brain defragmentation.

A week that was nothing less than a roller-coaster ride. The highs were creating my first agent, completing a 40-hour fast, and getting better at Python. The lows were two days of being unwell, not being able to write a few emails I wanted to, and not having enough time or energy.

My father’s death anniversary was an intensely emotional moment. I wrote a private letter to him that I wish I had written a couple of years back, when he was still here. I realized that the guilt of not being able to express our emotions to our father can feel permanent. At the end of the day, the only solace is that, as my father, I am sure he would have understood my situation and forgiven me for what I could not do or say. I wish we had the wisdom to do or say what we are meant to, every time. Why is it that we realize we were wrong only after such a long time, when we can’t repair it?

With this emotional elephant out of my mind and on paper, I felt good celebrating Shivaratri this year. I did a fast that I had wanted to do for a long time. It starts at sunset the previous day and ends at sunrise the next day, which is roughly a 40-hour fast. I believe internal energy (a loose translation of prana) gets overused through metabolic activities. When we pause those metabolic activities, our prana has enough energy to be regulated and moved upward to align with cosmic energy. Here, internal energy is called Shiva and cosmic energy is called Shakti. Shiva moves upward through our primary seven nervous plexuses (chakras) when we sit with our spine straight and keep our mind calm and undistracted. This is the purpose of Shivaratri, and fortunately it fell on a Sunday, when I had the freedom to do nothing.

The mistake I made was that when the fast ended on Monday, I should have ramped up food intake slowly. Instead, I ate normally right away, and that caused a severe stomach upset. Anyway, lessons learned, and it still feels like a great accomplishment in my own terms.

My recent love for building coding agents got a real start with my first coding agent. I built a Python coding agent that takes a prompt in text form and writes complete, structured, unit-tested Python code using the Claude API. You can read about it here. It is a 30-minute exercise, and the initial investment is $5. Here is the article for your reading pleasure and if you can build one yourself then give my article a clap.

I really like the way Anthropic is progressing. They are fast, agile, and world-class. A recent article by Marco Kotrotsos—Anthropic Is Running a Different Race—explained well why they are doing so well. They are definitely winning. I just hope they can sustain this for the long run.

The 90-day company

Strip away all the analysis and one thing stands out. Anthropic plans in 90-day cycles. They ship products in 10 days. They run on vibes and improv and the death of ego. And they’re outpacing companies with ten times their headcount.

This isn’t just a cute cultural quirk. It’s a competitive weapon.

Speaking of Anthropic, I discovered their agent “play store” (or app store). It’s amazing: 100+ agents, skills, and templates in one place, and they are free to use. It’s a great place to start if you want to see how agents work. You can access it here.

I know Python, but I have never taken a formal course. Right now, I am learning slowly and steadily, and it reminds me of my initial days learning C, C++, and Java. It feels better to learn step by step than to just code, because it helps you understand the “why” behind many things. My companion for that is Tutedude.com. They have interesting schemes where you get your money back if you complete the course within a stipulated period.

Another interesting article that resonated with what’s being discussed in tech circles in Bangalore is Why the Smartest People in Tech Are Quietly Panicking Right Now. For your reading pleasure. This is just a reaffirmation to what Matt Shumer wrote in his article or rather putting the same content in a different way. But below sentence caught my attention

Never in human history have the architects of our future been in such a state of existential panic, while the rest of the world casually complains that “the chatbot still can’t do math.”

I also got to consult a few friends on how to start their AI journey.

The steps I suggest are:

  1. Learn the basics of AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, and practice good prompt engineering.
    (I am designing a prompt engineering course. I know there are thousands available (and free), but I am creating one for the pleasure of creating.)
  2. Write about your learning and the benefits you observe, so you get community feedback and motivation.
  3. Build resources (AI resources like agents or your own flows) that make your life better, so that if someone asks why you talk about AI so much, you can show how it has helped you.

My friends find this useful, and I like the feeling too.

That’s a wrap for this fragment. See you all in the next one.

posts.html:
I built a Python Coding Agent from scratch this weekend.

Here’s the full playbook.

You type: “Create a function that analyzes a list of numbers.”
It returns: Working, production-ready Python code. In 3 seconds.

Here’s how I did it — and how you can replicate it in 30 minutes:

⚡ THE STACK (Surprisingly Simple)

  • Python 3.9+
  • anthropic library (the Claude API SDK)
  • python-dotenv (for API key safety)
  • That’s literally it.

🔑 5 STEPS TO BUILD IT:

1️⃣ Get your Anthropic API key from console.anthropic.com
→ Use Claude Haiku for cost efficiency (~$0.001 per generation)

2️⃣ Install dependencies
→ pip install anthropic python-dotenv

3️⃣ Write a system prompt (the agent’s “brain”)
→ “You are an expert Python developer. Write clean, well-commented code with error handling.”

4️⃣ Build the core generate_code() function
→ Sends your requirement to Claude → Extracts the code block → Saves to output folder

5️⃣ Add exponential backoff retry logic
→ Handles API overloads gracefully (Error 529 is real — I hit it on Day 1!)

💰 COST REALITY CHECK

  • 100 code generations/day = ~₹10/day
  • Claude Haiku: $0.25/million input tokens
  • One code generation: ~$0.001

This is the most cost-effective AI tool I’ve built.

🎁 BONUS FEATURES I added:
✅ Conversation memory — refine code iteratively
✅ Model switching — Haiku for speed, Sonnet for complexity
✅ Cost tracker — shows token usage after every call
✅ Auto-save — generated code saved to /output folder

Full open source code 👇
🔗 github.com/sakti1977/PythonAgent

Star the repo if this was useful. I have made it a public repo. Feel free to find issues, suggest enhancements or optimize.

posts.title: Fragments #1 — Defragmenting My Mind
posts.seoTitle: Fragments #1 — Defragmenting My Mind – Life as Sakti
posts.description: There's a technology blogger I deeply admire — Martin Fowler. The man doesn't just write about technology. He lives it, breathes it, and shares it the way a musician hums a tune they can't get out of their head. One thing he does is a blog series called Fragments — a collection of thoughts, articles,…
posts.html:
There’s a technology blogger I deeply admire — Martin Fowler. The man doesn’t just write about technology. He lives it, breathes it, and shares it the way a musician hums a tune they can’t get out of their head. One thing he does is a blog series called Fragments — a collection of thoughts, articles, and random musings from wildly different genres, all bundled together. The kind of writing that makes you peek into someone’s head and think, “Oh, this person thinks the same strange things I do.”

That idea stuck with me. My mind is always full — cluttered with half-formed ideas, things I’ve read, things I felt, things I haven’t yet put into words. In the world of computers, we’d call this state fragmented. And writing, I’ve decided, is my defragmentation tool.

So here we are. Fragment #1.

The Line That Wouldn’t Leave Me

This morning, I was reading Selected Poems of Oscar Wilde, and one section simply refused to let me go:

“Yet each man kills the thing he loves, By each let this be heard, Some do it with a bitter look, Some with a flattering word, The coward does it with a kiss, The brave man with a sword!”

I kept reading, and with every stanza, the weight of it grew heavier:

“Some kill their love when they are young, And some when they are old; Some strangle with the hands of Lust, Some with the hands of Gold: The kindest use a knife, because The dead so soon grow cold.

Some love too little, some too long, Some sell, and others buy; Some do the deed with many tears, And some without a sigh: For each man kills the thing he loves, Yet each man does not die.”

— Excerpt from Selected Poems of Oscar Wilde

There’s a painful truth buried in those lines. How often do we kill the very things we love — not with violence, but with neglect? A hobby abandoned. A relationship suffocated under silence. Gratitude lost in routine. Expectations that slowly strangle the joy out of something once cherished.

Wilde wrote it as a ballad about a prisoner. But it reads like a mirror held up to all of us.

The AI Toy That Reorganized My Life

Here’s something I didn’t expect to be writing about: Claude Code and Claude Cowork have become my newest obsessions.

I had folders. Decades of folders. Documents, notes, articles, saved resources — a digital archaeology site of my past interests and intentions. I always meant to go through them. I never did.

One prompt. One permission.

Claude Cowork walked through all of it and reorganized my digital life in a way I hadn’t been able to do in years. The realization that hit me afterward? Ninety percent of what I had saved wasn’t worth keeping. But the remaining ten percent? That ten percent contains enough material to fuel my writing for a very long time.

There’s a lesson in there about decluttering — not just of digital folders, but of mental space. When you stop hoarding everything, you start seeing what actually matters.

Yes, giving an AI agent access to your computer carries some risk. My trust threshold is admittedly lower than most people’s. But these folders held nothing private or confidential — just the accumulated weight of a curious mind that saved too much and processed too little.

If you want to understand what Cowork really is, read “Claude Cowork is a Game-Changer“ by Marco Kotrotsos on Medium. He captures something most coverage misses: Anthropic isn’t just making Claude more accessible to non-developers — they’re building a platform. The same Agent SDK, the same Skills framework, the same Connectors architecture. Developers got this first through Claude Code, and they’ve been quietly reaping productivity gains of 16–30% (per recent McKinsey research on AI adoption in software development). Now everyone else gets to play too.

The shift Marco describes is worth sitting with: we’re moving from “I do this task with AI assistance” to “I design systems where AI does this task.” The human stops being the executor. The human becomes the architect.

A Story That Explains the Unexplainable

On the quieter side of my reading life, I’m currently deep in Maha Brahmana by Devudu Narasimha Shastry — a celebrated Kannada novel that traces the spiritual transformation of King Kaushika into the sage Vishwamitra.

What fascinates me isn’t the mythology — it’s the craft. Devudu takes some of the most complex spiritual concepts in Vedic tradition, including the nature of the Gayatri mantra and the meaning of self-realization, and wraps them inside a story. Suddenly, the difficult becomes accessible. The abstract becomes human.

This is something I want to learn. The best teachers throughout history didn’t lecture — they told stories. Siddhartha and the arrow. The prodigal son. The Mahabharata itself. If a truth can’t be made into a narrative, it will usually be forgotten. If it can, it lives for millennia.

The Future Has Already Arrived

I’ve been meaning to write a long piece about how AI will reshape our world — the timeline, the implications, the human cost and the human potential. But then I came across “Something Big Is Happening“ by Matt Shumer, and he said what I wanted to say, better than I could have.

One passage from it stopped me cold:

“We’re past the point where this is an interesting dinner conversation about the future. The future is already here. It just hasn’t knocked on your door yet. It’s about to.”

That’s it. That’s the whole thing.

This isn’t a fad. The technology works. It improves predictably. The richest institutions in the world are committing trillions to it. And the people who will navigate this best aren’t the ones who understand it most technically — they’re the ones who start engaging with it now, with curiosity instead of fear, with urgency instead of comfort.

The disruption isn’t coming. It’s here. Most of us just haven’t felt the knock yet.

Closing Thought

So that’s my first Fragment — Oscar Wilde and Claude Cowork, ancient spiritual wisdom and the AI revolution, all living together in the same mind on the same Tuesday morning.

Perhaps that’s the most human thing about all of this: we are never just one thing. We are always, always, fragments.

posts.title: Letting Go of Toxic Friendships Gracefully
posts.seoTitle: Letting Go of Toxic Friendships Gracefully – Life as Sakti
posts.description: There's something magical about the moment you realize friendship isn't just about having people around you—it's about the energy they bring into your life.
