routes.seoTitle: Anger (negative) – Life as Sakti
routes.description: I must be mad to think about ‘Anger’ on the day love is in the air all over the world. But I think it is very much necessary to understand anger any day. Anger has various flavors. Some are positive and some are negative. Here I am talking about negative anger. Human body understands anger…
routes.html:
I must be mad to think about ‘Anger’ on the day love is in the air all over the world. But I think it is very much necessary to understand anger any day. Anger has various flavors. Some are positive and some are negative. Here I am talking about negative anger.

Human body understands anger very well. It gives you many signals to indicate that you are angry. Some common signs are Face turning red, sweating especially palms, shivering, unclear or shaky voice, loud voice, things falling from hands, throwing things etc. Here our body is trying to indicate that something is wrong. When our body indicates anything it means we need to take some necessary action. But we hardly care what our body tell us.

We get angry with people, objects, ourselves, and sometime entire world. The reason for getting angry is not necessary to describe but there is one thing common in all reasons i.e. not happy. Have you ever seen anybody happy but still angry? I have never. And we are not happy because something happened or happening against our expectations. Our expectation may be legitimate or utter non-sense. Whatever may be the situation or reason, anger (negative) is neither good for us nor anybody around us. Have you ever found a solution when you are angry? I have never so far.

The output of the ‘anger’ process is always hurting ourselves and/or others really hard either physically or emotionally. Most of the time we hurt ourselves more than others and we loose more than the other person. We may realize what we lost after sometime but the time would have gone by then to rectify that. When we hurt somebody emotionally it takes years to heal and most of the times it never heals.

You mostly get angry and upset with your loved ones very often. You get angry for some silly reasons and you react to situations badly. The reason is you have many expectations from them. You assume they understand your situation as you do but it is not humanly possible to do so.  No human in this world can ever understand what you are going through as you do. I would exclude Mother’s here because they are next to god  and they know everything. Stay away from your loved ones for sometime you will regret what you have done big time and you can never forgive yourself.

Then we get angry with people at work or society. Again here expectation is the cause for the anger but once we build an impression about them it remain there for long. After that whatever they do you dislike that, even if they do it with good intentions. You become skeptical . But if the same is done by another person whom we like, we don’t mind.

Most of the times anger goes off when we understand the situation from the other persons point of view.  Can we do this while getting angry, so that, we do not get angry and manage the situation better? Yes it is possible with lots of practice and by keeping your expectations flexible. Thinking before reacting can help us understand the situation better and handle it. But here factor that plays a role is time. How much time we give to think before we react. generally we get angry at the very moment. Have you ever see a situation where something happened and you got angry after few hours? Never. But if you practice to do that then you may succeed in managing your anger.

– Stray Dog

routes.title: Drowning in Abundance: My Life at the Edge of the AI Age
routes.seoTitle: Drowning in Abundance: My Life at the Edge of the AI Age – Life as Sakti
routes.description: For the past several months, I have been reading, practicing, and writing about AI — obsessively, almost embarrassingly. And then Claude and OpenAI dropped their latest releases. Claude Cowork arrived. And something shifted. Earlier, my head was a crowded marketplace of ideas with almost no hands to execute them. Now, the hands are faster than…
routes.html:
For the past several months, I have been reading, practicing, and writing about AI — obsessively, almost embarrassingly. And then Claude and OpenAI dropped their latest releases. Claude Cowork arrived. And something shifted.

Earlier, my head was a crowded marketplace of ideas with almost no hands to execute them. Now, the hands are faster than the ideas. That is a strange and wonderful problem to have.

Here is the first sign I noticed something had fundamentally changed in me: I stopped hitting my daily limits on Instagram and YouTube.

For nearly a year, I had set a strict 30-minute cap on both — a small act of sanity in a noisy world. I held that boundary like a promise to myself. But in the past few days, I haven’t even come close to the limit. Not because I am suppressing the urge. Simply because I don’t feel the pull anymore. Practicing, reading, and writing about AI has quietly replaced the scroll.

I got busier. But it’s a different kind of busy.

You know that feeling when you plan a vacation hoping to do absolutely nothing — to just lie on a beach, stare at the sky, let your mind go blank? And then you find yourself hiking at 6 AM, exploring every corner of the city, physically exhausted but oddly alive?

That’s exactly what AI is doing to my calendar.

It was supposed to free up time. And it does — in pockets. But those pockets don’t stay empty for long. They fill up with new experiments, new projects, new questions. Every block of freed time becomes a canvas. The abundance is almost overwhelming.

It feels like a jumbo buffet opening its doors to someone who hasn’t eaten in days. You don’t slow down. You load the plate.

Last week, I turned that energy toward my WordPress website.

I used to spend hours — sometimes entire evenings — editing layouts, customizing pages, wrestling with plugins. It was a labor of love, but labor nonetheless. This time, with AI as my co-pilot, I transformed the pages in minutes.

And then I sat back and asked myself a question that felt slightly absurd given where I was writing it: Do I even need WordPress anymore?

Yes, I realize the irony. Writing a “why I might leave WordPress” post on WordPress. The universe has a sense of humor.

But here is the truth: if I have a domain, I can build pages and host them. It’s not as plug-and-play as WordPress, but with a little discipline and curiosity — both of which seem to be in good supply these days — it is entirely possible. The gatekeeping is gone.

I also built an MCP — a small but satisfying project — that takes a finished blog post and generates shareable content for LinkedIn, Facebook, Twitter, and WhatsApp in one go. My social media posting time is now close to zero.

The tools are falling into place. The workflow is tightening.

But here is what I have realized stays irreplaceable in all of this: original thought.

AI can amplify an idea. It can execute, refine, and distribute it at speed. But the spark — the original observation, the genuine insight, the lived experience — that still has to come from somewhere human. From somewhere inside.

So I am carving out 2.5 hours every day just to read.

Not online articles. Not newsletters. Books. Physical, distraction-free, margin-scribbling books. Because that is where I find the quiet necessary for real absorption. That is where original ideas still have room to breathe.

I am sharing this not as a productivity prescription, but simply as a snapshot of one person’s state of mind in the middle of a strange and exciting moment in history.

If any of this resonates with you — if you too are standing at this same buffet, plate in hand, slightly overwhelmed but smiling — let’s give each other a quiet thumbs up.

We are figuring this out together.

routes.title: The Morning Before the World Woke Up
routes.seoTitle: The Morning Before the World Woke Up – Life as Sakti
routes.description: How One Page a Day from India's Ancient Wisdom Traditions Can Change Everything A woman captures a quiet moment of reading as the sun rises over a misty mountain range. It was 4:47 AM when I first read the line that broke me open. Not "broke" in the dramatic sense. Broke like a seed breaks…
routes.html:
How One Page a Day from India’s Ancient Wisdom Traditions Can Change Everything

It was 4:47 AM when I first read the line that broke me open.

Not “broke” in the dramatic sense. Broke like a seed breaks — that quiet, underground rupture before something green pushes through.

The verse was from the Bhagavad Gita. Just one. I hadn’t planned to change my life that morning. I had only planned to wake up before the noise started.

A Book a Day Was a Lie I Told Myself

We’ve all been there. The bookshelf that doubles as a monument to good intentions. The highlighted pages we’ll “go back to.” The productivity guru who swears by reading 52 books a year.

I tried. I failed. And somewhere between trying and failing, I missed the entire point.

The ancient traditions of India never asked you to consume wisdom. They asked you to sit with it. To let it breathe inside you. To carry it like a lamp into the ordinary Tuesday of your life.

Ryan Holiday built an empire of morning rituals around Stoic philosophy — one quote, one reflection, one journal entry. The remarkable thing is, he was doing what the Guru Granth Sahib already knew. What the Dhammapada already knew. What the rishis sitting in forest hermitages thousands of years ago already practiced.

They called it Svadhyaya — self-study through sacred reading.

One page was always enough.

The Story of the River and the Stone

There is an old image that returns to me often: water doesn’t break stone through force. It breaks stone through return. The same gentle pressure, again and again, over time, until the hardest surface yields.

A page a day is not about information. It is about return.

You return to the Yoga Vasistha and its wild, luminous claim that the world you perceive is a dream the mind is having. You return to Rumi’s Masnavi — not to understand it, but to be confused by it in a slightly different way than yesterday. You return to the Japji Sahib, whose opening line asks a question so large it takes a lifetime to hear: How do we become truthful before the One who is Truth itself?

Each morning, you return. And slowly — imperceptibly, like a stone beside a river — you change.

The Texts That Were Always Designed for This

Here is what most people don’t realize: India’s greatest philosophical texts were never meant to be read cover to cover in an airport lounge.

The Dhammapada is 423 verses. The Buddha’s distilled teaching on how to live. Two verses a morning and you’ve spent a year walking beside the most awake mind in human history.

The Upanishads — those radical, dazzling inquiries into the nature of consciousness — were oral traditions passed from teacher to student one insight at a time. Eknath Easwaran, one of their most beloved translators, structured his commentary explicitly as daily readings. He understood the original architecture.

The Yoga Vasistha Sara, the distilled essence of one of India’s longest philosophical epics, fits in your palm. A paragraph before breakfast, and you are suddenly wondering what the word “I” actually refers to. Good. That is the point.

The Masnavi of Rumi — Sufi wisdom in the form of story, metaphor, and poetry — rewards slowness. One story, one couplet. Let it echo through your afternoon.

The Japji Sahib from the Guru Granth Sahib was not written to be finished. It was written to be lived. It is the first prayer of the Sikh day, recited by millions each dawn, its cadences worn smooth by generations of devoted return.

These are not books. They are companions.

The Ritual (And Why It Has to Be Small)

The enemy of transformation is ambition.

We set the alarm for 5 AM, pull out the leather-bound journal, light the lap, and commit to an hour of morning philosophy. It works for nine days. Then life happens. Then we feel like failures. Then the book goes back on the shelf.

The tradition asks for something far less heroic, and far more powerful.

One page. One verse. One story.

Here is the practice, stripped to its bones:

Before your phone tells you what to think, before the inbox makes its demands, before the world inserts its agenda into your morning — open the text. Read one page. Not two. One.

Then close the book. Sit for a moment. Ask yourself: What does this have to do with what I’m walking into today?

Write the answer down. Even three sentences. Even one.

That’s it.

You’ve just done something the Vedic tradition considers sacred. You’ve practiced Svadhyaya. You’ve watered the inner life before the outer one makes its noise.

What Changes (And When)

Nothing changes at first. This is important to know.

Week one, you feel slightly philosophical and mildly self-congratulatory. Week two, you miss two days and feel guilty. Week three, something shifts. You’re in a difficult meeting and a line from the Gita surfaces — “You have a right to perform your prescribed duties, but you are not entitled to the fruits of your actions” — and instead of tightening with anxiety, you feel something release.

That’s when you understand what the tradition was trying to give you all along.

Not information. Equanimity. Not knowledge. A way to stand inside your own life without being consumed by it.

By month three, the practice has become structural — like brushing your teeth, but for the part of you that asks why am I doing any of this?

Which Text Do You Choose?

Start with one. Just one. For a year.

If you are drawn to the question of action — what it means to do your duty without attachment to outcomes — begin with the Bhagavad Gita. There are beautiful daily-reading editions organized by Ravi Ravindra and others, 700 verses mapped to 365 mornings.

If you are drawn to the question of consciousness — what the mind is, what “I” is, whether the dreamer and the dream are different — enter the Upanishads through Easwaran’s patient, brilliant commentary.

If you are drawn to the question of suffering and release — how to live with loss, with change, with the impossibility of holding anything — sit each morning with the Dhammapada.

If you are drawn to the heart, the longing, the ache of something vast inside a small life — let Rumi’s Masnavi be your companion.

If you want a daily practice that has been tested by millions of lives across five centuries — begin the Japji Sahib. Let its rhythm become the rhythm of your mornings.

A Word About What This Is Not

This is not about becoming spiritual in a way that floats above ordinary life.

The Gita was spoken on a battlefield. The Dhammapada was offered to people struggling with jealousy, grief, and fear. The Masnavi is full of imperfect, stumbling human beings finding grace in the most ridiculous circumstances.

This is a practice for the person who has a 9 AM standup. For the person who is navigating a difficult manager, a difficult relationship, a difficult self. For the senior leader who has every credential and still wonders, in the quiet moments, if they are building something that matters.

One page a day is not an escape from that life. It is the practice of meeting it with a little more of yourself intact.

The Morning Ritual, Reclaimed

Somewhere in Bengaluru, or Chennai, or any city where the traffic starts early and the day hits hard — a morning is happening right now where someone woke up before the noise began.

They made chai. They sat near the window. They opened a worn copy of the Dhammapada, or the Yoga Vasistha Sara, or the Guru Granth Sahib. They read one page.

They are not a saint. They are not a philosopher. They are just someone who decided, quietly, that the inner life deserved five minutes before the outer one claimed the rest.

And day by day — like water on stone, like a seed breaking underground — they are becoming someone slightly more awake than before.

One page was enough.

It always was.

The texts mentioned in this piece — the Bhagavad Gita, Upanishads, Yoga Vasistha Sara, Dhammapada, Masnavi, Conference of the Birds, Tattvartha Sutra, and Japji Sahib — are among the most profound works in human history. Each tradition has its own commentary lineage; seek out translators like Eknath Easwaran, Ravi Ravindra, and Jawid Mojaddedi for accessible, scholarly, and deeply human entry points.

If this resonated, I write regularly about leadership, technology, and the examined life. Connect with me on LinkedIn or explore more at saktibagchi.in.

routes.title: Experience Changes How You Prompt
routes.seoTitle: Experience Changes How You Prompt – Life as Sakti
routes.description: Unlocking the Power of Experience: How Prompting in AI Can Elevate Your Knowledge! A seasoned professional demonstrates advanced AI-assisted workflows in a modern office environment. A junior developer sees AI as a shortcut. I see it as a collaborator. Here is why experience changes everything about how you prompt. In my first job in Bangalore…
routes.html:
Unlocking the Power of Experience: How Prompting in AI Can Elevate Your Knowledge!

A junior developer sees AI as a shortcut. I see it as a collaborator. Here is why experience changes everything about how you prompt.

In my first job in Bangalore in 2000, I was a software engineer trainee with a simple belief: if I could think logically, step by step, everything would fall into place.

Then I met my first real blocker.

My manager would not let me send emails.

Not “try harder” or “be careful”. Literally: no emails to our US counterparts. No code check-ins. No commits. And I was furious.

I remember thinking: This is exactly why people say managers are bad.

But the reality was more nuanced, and it taught me the most enduring lesson of my career.

The two-hour email

Our US counterparts sat in Tucson, Arizona. The overlap window was small.

If we asked the wrong question, or communicated poorly, the cost was not “some back-and-forth”. The cost was a full day.

So my manager would do something that felt ridiculous at the time.

They made me sit next to them for up to two hours, rewriting a single email.

First question:

“What do you want as a response?”

My answer was always some version of:

“I want them to either approve the design or tell me if I am fundamentally wrong.”

Then the editing began.

They would reorder sentences.

They would delete a line I felt was “important”.

They would highlight one sentence and say, “This is the only thing they need to respond to.”

By the time we hit send, my original email barely existed.

At first, I read it as power.

Later, I saw it as craft.

Because the responses we got back were exactly what we needed. Approval. Or a clear correction. In minutes. Inside that thin overlap window.

That email saved days.

And eventually, after about a year of this, my manager let me write and send emails on my own.

The surprising part is: I have been using that same mental model ever since.

A concrete AI example: two prompts, two different worlds

Fast-forward to today.

A junior developer on a team will often treat AI like a vending machine.

They type something like:

“Can you write a design for this feature?”

They get something clean, confident, and… generic.

It sounds correct because it is written well. But it does not engage with the real risks.

It does not ask the hard questions.

It does not reveal what it does not know.

Now here is the “experienced” version of the same task.

Instead of asking for “a design”, I ask the AI to play the role I need, with the constraints I actually have.

“You are a senior engineer reviewing a design proposal. Context: we have only a 30–60 minute overlap with the US team, so we need to minimize back-and-forth. Goal: produce a one-page design email that gets an approval or a specific correction in one reply.

Feature: [brief description].

Constraints: [existing system, latency, data model, whatever is real].

Please:

  1. Ask the 5 most important clarifying questions first.
  1. Then draft the email in a format that makes it easy to approve.
  1. Include a short “what could go wrong” section with 3–5 risks.”

The difference is not the model.

The difference is that the second prompt contains:

  • Context
  • A clear outcome
  • A defined role
  • Constraints
  • A response format
  • And most importantly: a sensitivity to the cost of a bad response

The real insight: prompting well requires knowing what “bad” looks like

A junior developer can be smart and hardworking and still struggle to prompt well.

Not because they lack vocabulary.

Because prompting is not just about asking.

It is about recognizing.

Recognizing when an answer is:

  • technically plausible but operationally impossible
  • correct in theory but risky in practice
  • missing the one question that will block the project later
  • confidently vague

That recognition takes time.

It comes from getting burned by ambiguity.

It comes from sending the wrong email and losing a day.

It comes from seeing a project drift because nobody forced clarity at the start.

In other words:

Prompting well requires knowing what a bad answer looks like.

And that knowledge takes years.

Why I no longer see AI as a shortcut

AI is powerful, but it is not magic.

If you treat it like a shortcut, you will mostly get shortcuts back.

If you treat it like a collaborator, you will start doing what good collaborators do:

  • you give context
  • you align on outcomes
  • you define constraints
  • you ask for the response format you need
  • you iterate with intention

That is not “prompt engineering”.

That is simply communication.

It is the same lesson my manager taught me, one two-hour email at a time.

One question to close

What has your experience taught AI that a textbook could not?

routes.html:
How an AI reading loop forced me to finally bring my house — my mind — in order

Act I — The Loop That Wouldn’t Stop

It started, like most dangerous things in my life, with a good idea.

I had built a reading loop — AI-assisted, naturally. Every morning I would feed articles into Claude, ask it to summarise, extract insights, and suggest what I should write next. Then I’d draft a piece. Claude would refine it. I’d publish. The loop was elegant. The loop was productive. The loop was, I told myself, the future of knowledge work.

What I didn’t notice — not for the first few weeks, anyway — was that the loop had a flaw baked into its very elegance.

I was reading more than ever. Writing more than ever. But I had quietly stopped finishing things. A Medium draft sat at 80% for eleven days. A GitHub repo that needed three more commits gathered dust. An email to my cross-geo team about the upcoming PI planning sat as a red unread reminder in my own inbox.

I had optimised the intake. I had forgotten to optimise the output.

That sentence — scribbled in the margin of a notebook while waiting for a CI pipeline to finish — became the pivot point of everything that followed.

Act II — The Cheatsheet on the Wall

A colleague shared Dr. Miro Bada’s infographic: How to Master Time Management — The Cheatsheet to Win Back Your Time. Fifteen frameworks on a single page. I had seen most of them before, scattered across blog posts and productivity books. But seeing them all together, in one visual, did something different to my brain.

It felt like walking into a cluttered room and suddenly having someone turn on all the lights at once.

I printed it. I stuck it on the wall beside my monitor. And for the first time in weeks, I stopped reading and started looking — really looking — at how I was spending my hours.

Here is what I found, and here is what I did about it.

Act III — Fifteen Mirrors, One Reflection

1. The Domino Effect — Stop Starting, Start Sequencing

My calendar was a museum of parallel beginnings. Three architectural documents in draft. Two LinkedIn posts half-written. One book chapter stalled at a metaphor I couldn’t crack.

The Domino Effect asks a simple question: which task, when completed, makes the next one easier? I restructured my week around this logic. The PI planning summary first — because it unblocked five team leads. The Medium article second — because finishing it cleared the mental noise. The GitHub commits third — because they were small and fast, the kind of domino that falls in ten minutes and makes you feel human again.

2. The 1-3-5 Rule — The Morning Contract

I began writing a daily contract with myself. One big thing. Three medium things. Five small things. Not a wishlist — a contract. The difference is accountability.

The AI loop actually helps here: I now ask Claude each morning to help me triage the day’s tasks into this structure. It takes four minutes. It saves two hours of drift.

3. The Not-Todo List — The Art of Strategic Abandonment

This one stung.

I identified six recurring tasks that I was doing out of habit, not value. Three I automated. Two I delegated to team members who were frankly better at them than I was. One I simply eliminated — a weekly report nobody was reading.

Freedom, it turns out, is sometimes just a deleted calendar invite.

4. Airplane Mode — The Sacred Window

Between 6:30 AM and 8:00 AM, my phone goes into airplane mode. No Slack. No email. No news. This is when I read, write, and think. The AI loop now lives entirely in this window. Claude gets my full attention. In return, I get my full morning.

5. The 5-Second Rule — Launching Into the Uncomfortable

5-4-3-2-1. Launch.

I use this specifically for the tasks I have been avoiding — the difficult feedback email, the architectural decision document that required me to admit I had been wrong about something for three months. The countdown is ridiculous. It works anyway.

6. S.M.A.R.T Goals — Making the Fuzzy Concrete

My AI reading loop was not SMART. It had no defined endpoint, no measurable output, no time boundary. I added one rule: every reading session must produce one publishable insight within 48 hours. Suddenly, the loop had a shape.

7. The Seesaw System — Balancing the High and the Low

Architecture reviews and PI planning are cognitively heavy. Reviewing pull requests and updating documentation are lighter. I now interleave them deliberately — heavy task, light task, heavy task, light task. My energy curve stopped looking like a cliff and started looking like a wave.

8. The 80/20 Rule — Finding the Vital Few

Twenty percent of my tasks drive eighty percent of my professional impact. For me, that twenty percent is: strategic documents, key stakeholder communications, and the Medium articles that shape my thought leadership positioning.

I put those tasks in the morning. Everything else gets the afternoon.

9. Task Batching — The Context-Switch Tax

Every time you switch contexts, you pay a tax. I was paying it dozens of times a day. Now I batch: all code reviews in one block, all writing in one block, all meetings compressed into Tuesday and Thursday afternoons. The rest of the week breathes.

10. Eat Your Frog — The Hardest Thing First

My frog changes daily. Some days it is a difficult conversation. Some days it is a blank document that needs 800 words I do not yet have. Some days it is simply getting out of bed early enough to have a morning at all.

I eat it first. Always. The rest of the day tastes better for it.

11. The Eisenhower Matrix — Triage as a Discipline

I built a simple habit: every Sunday evening, I run the week’s tasks through the matrix. Urgent + Important gets my mornings. Important + Not Urgent gets scheduled. Urgent + Not Important gets delegated. Not Important + Not Urgent gets deleted without guilt.

The matrix does not give you more time. It gives you better decisions about the time you have.

12. The Unfinished Symphony — The Power of Beginning

I had always been afraid to start things I could not finish in one sitting. The Unfinished Symphony principle inverted this. Now I deliberately start things — a paragraph, a diagram, a code stub — knowing I will not finish them today. The brain, it turns out, does not like loose ends. It works on them in the background, whether you ask it to or not.

Several of my best Medium paragraphs were written in the shower, solving a problem I started the night before.

13. The Pomodoro Technique — Time as Ritual

25 minutes. 5-minute break. Repeat. I pair this with the Airplane Mode window for deep work. What I discovered: the technique is not really about time. It is about permission — permission to stop, permission to rest, permission to begin again.

14. Time Blocking — Designing the Day

My calendar now has three types of blocks: Deep Work (marked in blue, non-negotiable), Collaborative Work (meetings, reviews, team calls), and Recovery (lunch, walk, nothing-in-particular). The third category was the hardest to add. It was the most important.

15. Power Hour + Closing the Day — The Bookends

I begin with a Power Hour: one uninterrupted hour on the week’s most important project. I end with a Closing ritual: wrap up open loops, review what I completed, write three priorities for tomorrow.

The closing ritual, specifically, changed how I sleep. The open loops were not keeping me awake — I had just never given myself a formal place to put them down.

Act IV — What the AI Loop Looks Like Now

The loop did not disappear. It matured.

I still use Claude every morning. I still read, synthesise, and write. But now the loop has a container: it lives in the Airplane Mode window, structured by the 1-3-5 rule, launched by the 5-Second Rule, and bounded by a Power Hour timer. The Eisenhower Matrix decides whether a new reading topic earns a slot in my week. The Domino Effect decides the sequence.

The result: I publish more, drift less, and finish what I start.

The frameworks in Dr. Bada’s cheatsheet are not new ideas. Most of them are decades old. What is new — what I believe is the essential skill for anyone building in the age of AI — is the discipline to apply them when the tools around you are actively rewarding distraction with the illusion of productivity.

Reading faster is not the same as thinking better.

Writing more is not the same as writing well.

A loop that generates output is not the same as a mind that has direction.

Coda — Bringing the House in Order

The Bhagavad Gita speaks of chitta-shuddhi — the purification of the mind, the clearing of the inner house before any great work can be done. I am not a philosopher. I am an engineering manager with a backlog and a calendar and a persistent sense that there is more I could be doing with the hours I have.

But I have come to believe that the frameworks above are a modern chitta-shuddhi. They are not productivity tricks. They are acts of respect — for your own attention, for your team’s time, for the work that deserves to be done well.

The AI will keep reading. The AI will keep writing. The AI will keep suggesting what comes next.

But the architect of that loop — the one who decides what gets built, and when, and why — that has to be you.

Bring your house in order. Then build.

For the past several months, I have been consuming at a breakneck speed. My "diet" has been a relentless stream of LinkedIn insights,…
routes.html:
In biology, the cycle is simple: you consume, you digest, and you excrete. If any part of that system fails, you get sick.

I’ve realized the same applies to our digital lives.

For the past several months, I have been consuming at a breakneck speed. My “diet” has been a relentless stream of LinkedIn insights, Medium deep-dives, X threads, and niche blogs. But without a way to process it, all that consumption resulted in a kind of “intellectual heartburn”—discomfort, confusion, and a cluttered mind.

The Digestion Phase

To settle the heartburn, I started building. Digestion, for me, is the act of turning passive consumption into active creation. I moved from being a spectator to an architect, building projects ranging from the sentimental to the ambitious:

  • A Bengali Calendar app for my mother.
  • A custom MCP to manage my social media presence.
  • Reviving my incomplete book manuscripts.
  • An AI Agent specifically for Python coding.
  • A “Deep Research & Fake Filter” to clean up my daily information intake.

This is on top of my day-to-day at Altera, where I live in GitHub Copilot. For my personal projects, I’ve moved from Claude Code to experimenting with Anti Gravity.

Building has helped. The confusion is clearing. But it has created a new problem: I am glued to my chair, day and night. I feel fragmented.

The Necessity of Excretion

This is where the third step comes in: Excretion. To maintain a healthy mental ecosystem, I have to let go. I have to purge the noise to make room for what matters.

My “Excretion Policy” moving forward:

  1. The “No” List: A strict policy on what I will not consume anymore. If it doesn’t add value to my core goals, it’s out.
  2. AI Fasting: Scheduled time where I am completely out of the loop. No models, no prompts, no screens.
  3. Tool Monogamy: I’ve decided to master one tool at a time until I’ve exhausted its utility. Jumping between every new shiny AI tool leads to a satisfied ego but a shallow understanding.
  4. Hand-Coding as Vitality: I am re-learning Python, Rust, and Go through various platforms, not just to generate code, but to understand it deeply enough to write it by hand. It’s about keeping my own cognitive “muscles” alive while the AI does the heavy lifting.

It’s been a fascinating journey so far, but the lesson is clear: If you want to stay sane in the age of AI, you cannot just consume.

Consume. Digest. Excrete. Repeat for system health.

routes.seoTitle: Etiquette – Life as Sakti

Lift reached our floor and opened. People came out of it as if their survival was compromised inside the lift. People standing outside were eager to enter…
routes.html:
Namaste!!!

Standing in front of the 7 Seas mall lower basement lift to go to the top floor. Navneel was holding my hand and Hiya was standing little far away. Lift reached our floor and opened. People came out of it as if their survival was compromised inside the lift. People standing outside were eager to enter as if there is a gold biscuit distribution inside the lift on first come first serve basis. I being an arrogant first class citizen of Bharat with lots of pseudo etiquette in my head, was standing to get my turn holding Navneel’s hand tightly so that he does not run to get inside the lift. But I forgot that he has cosmic energy in him and I was having only food energy. His energy defeated mine and he ran inside the lift finding way through the gaps in between legs. He went inside and secured a place for himself and started his experiment on truth. I got the chance to be the last one in the crowd and had to sand in such a position that lift door brushed through my nose tip while closing. But I did not let my spine bend or arrogance soften.

Hiya observing all these asked, “Baba, why didn’t you try to go early then we could have secured a better place inside the lift.”. I said proudly and in a grave voice, “This is etiquette.”. By the time she was processing this word with 3Ts in this word, We were out of the lift in one of the floors where there are many shops. We walked towards a shop and I pulled the handle of the door to open it. There were many people who were inside the shop started walking out as if they were waiting for me to open the door. Hiya and Navneel tried to push them to go inside but I held them back. Then those people came out leisurely. The only thing missing was, me telling them ‘Thank you’ or saluting them. One gentleman walking out using his most precious organ (i.e. Cellphone) and stood just at the door to think before speaking. He took his time as his time is his own. I stood there with a smile and waited for him. So finally when I saw nobody was coming outside, I let the kids go and then I walked inside. This time Hiya asked, “Baba, why were you waiting for them to come out? You could have gone inside first as you opened the door.”. I smiled at her and said, “Etiquette, Mamma! Etiquette”.

She continued her thought on this subject till we crashed on bed after returning back. She asked me “Baba, Why we need to show etiquette and why only you were showing etiquette?”. I said, “Everybody should show etiquette. May be nobody taught them.”. She asked again, “But, why do we need to show etiquette?”. This time the emphasis was on ‘Why’. This made me think. I have shown etiquette till date because somebody taught me when I was a kid but I never thought ‘Why?’ till date. The response that I gave immediately was, “We must follow etiquettes so that we do not cause discomfort to anybody. So that everybody in the society feels comfortable.”. Then she immediately questioned, “What about our comfort? It looks like etiquette is only for us to give comfort to others.”. This question was bit tough for me to answer. Then I referred to dictionary.

et-i-quette-

1.conventional requirements as to social behavior; proprieties of conduct as established in any class or community or for any occasion.

2.a prescribed or accepted code of usage in matters of ceremony, as at a court or in official or other formal observances.

3.the code of ethical behavior regarding professional practice or action among the members of a profession in their dealings with each other: medical etiquette.

Origin:
1740–50; < French étiquette, Middle French estiquette ticket, memorandum, derivative of estiqu ( i ) er to attach, stick < Germanic.

—Synonyms
1. Etiquette, decorum, propriety imply observance of the formal requirements governing behavior in polite society. Etiquette refers to conventional forms and usages: the rules of etiquette. Decorum suggests dignity and a sense of what is becoming or appropriate for a person of good breeding: a fine sense of decorum. Propriety (usually plural) implies established conventions of morals and good taste: She never fails to observe the proprieties

So, what I understood from it is, a code of conduct that is agreed upon by all in a polite society. Now question comes, Are we a polite society? Have we agreed upon a code of conduct? if Yes then this question should not arise and if not, then also this question should not arise.

Need help in understanding so that I can respond to Hiya? Please let me know your responses through comments.

Namaste!!

– Stray Dog

routes.title: The Singing Stray
routes.seoTitle: The Singing Stray – Life as Sakti

routes.html:
A confession in four humiliations and one glorious moment

I.

The headmaster made the announcement during morning prayers, the way headmasters always deliver news that will change the course of someone’s life — flatly, between the attendance register and the lunch break schedule.

“There is an inter-school song competition. All interested participants must go through a screen test. If you qualify, you will represent the school.”

The words floated over the courtyard, past the serious students already calculating their chances, past the talented ones already rehearsing in their heads, and landed — somehow — in mine.

I am not entirely sure what possessed me. I had no training. No particular talent that anyone, including myself, had ever noticed. I didn’t even have a song picked out. But there has always lived inside me a creature that perks up at the word competition the way a stray dog perks up at the smell of food — not because it has a plan, but because it simply cannot help itself.

So I went.

II.

The room was full of hopefuls. I sat among them, listening to each one step up, sing their piece, and step off — and I was still thinking about what I would sing. There is a particular kind of person who decides to improvise at a singing audition. I was that person.

When they called my name, I walked to the stage with the confidence of someone who has not yet understood what is about to happen to them.

The microphone looked simple enough. I leaned into it.

It shrieked.

The teacher looked up. “Keep some distance between the microphone and your mouth.”

I nodded and stepped back. And in that single, clumsy moment — the feedback, the correction, the entire room watching — I forgot the song. Every song. Every word of every song I had ever known in my entire life simply vacated my mind like passengers abandoning a sinking ship.

I stood there. Seconds passed. The kind of seconds that feel like they’ve been specially manufactured to be longer than normal.

“You can’t stand there forever,” my teacher said, not unkindly, though it did not feel that way. “There are others waiting.”

The only thing that surfaced from the wreckage of my memory was the school prayer. Which I then sang — with, I must say, considerable soul — until the teacher raised his hand to stop me.

He was quiet for a moment. Then:

“Sa-re-ga-ma-pa-dha-ni — all coming together at the same time. Has nobody ever told you not to sing in public?” He paused for dramatic effect. “If nobody has, I am telling you now: never try singing ever. It is going to be hazardous for mankind.”

The room erupted. And I — because what else do you do when you are the punchline — laughed with them. Loudly. So they would think I was in on the joke, and not notice that some small part of me had just been quietly folded up and put away.

III.

Here is the strange thing. I never stopped.

Not on stages — I had learned my lessons about stages — but everywhere else. On window seats of buses and trains, with the landscape rolling past and nobody able to escape me. In quiet offices during slow afternoons. In rooms where people were too polite to say anything and simply pretended I wasn’t there, hoping the silence of their disapproval would extinguish me.

It never did.

I began to fancy that I sang with emotion, at least. I used to console myself with this privately: the notes may be wrong, but the feeling is right. Tolerant souls occasionally confirmed the first half of that theory. The second half, they left alone.

But the hunger — the specific, unreasonable hunger to sing on a stage, in front of real people, with a real microphone — that never went away. It just waited. The way all unreasonable hungers do.

IV. The Night of Helious

Engineering college brings with it many gifts. Freedom. Chaos. The terrifying discovery of who you actually are when nobody from your childhood is watching.

And for me — unexpectedly, beautifully — it brought Helious.

Helious was our college cultural festival. One of those annual explosions of colour, noise, terrible sound systems, and genuine joy that engineering colleges somehow produce better than anyone else. And in my final year, through a combination of persistence and the kind of enthusiastic volunteering that people mistake for competence, I found myself on the organizing committee.

I had the stage. I had the access. I had, for perhaps the first and last time in my life, control.

The poet in me had been writing in Odia for years — private lines, quiet verses that I kept mostly to myself. That year, I had set one of them to the melody of a popular Odia tune that everyone in the audience would recognize. I had been carrying this arrangement in my head for weeks, the way you carry something fragile, not quite believing it will survive the journey.

The night of the festival arrived. A thousand students filled the ground.

I walked to the microphone during a gap in the programme — calm the way only the truly deluded are calm — and I sang my poem. My words. My melody. My moment, finally, after all those years of bus windows and empty corridors and teachers telling me I was a hazard to mankind.

The stage lights were in my eyes. Bright, warm, absolute. Beyond them: darkness. A thousand people dissolved into a single, breathing shadow that I could hear but not see.

I finished.

Silence.

Not scattered applause, not the embarrassed murmuring of an audience unsure what they had witnessed. Silence. Complete and total.

Now, there are several explanations for this. The uncharitable ones involve acoustics, pitch, and the general welfare of the assembled crowd. But I prefer my own interpretation, which I have held onto carefully for many years now:

They were mesmerized.

A thousand engineers, the kinds of people trained to analyse, critique, and argue about everything — rendered speechless. By my poetry. By my voice. By the sheer unexpected audacity of a boy who had been told he was a hazard to mankind standing under the lights and singing his own words into the dark.

They simply forgot to clap.

It is, I think, the most likely explanation.

V.

Then came the colleague.

He approached me one afternoon with the careful expression of someone delivering difficult news to a child. “Sakti,” he said, “why don’t you try recording your songs? Or even — a radio station?”

Something inside me soared. I was milliseconds away from saying you know, I never had any formal training, but I always felt the music— when he finished his sentence.

“At least then I can switch off the radio.”

The room laughed. I laughed. We all laughed together, which is the great social mercy extended to those of us who are perpetually, lovably wrong about ourselves.

Coda

I still ask people, sometimes, “Don’t you feel the pain in the song when I sing?”

They always say yes. Always.

“Yes — in our ears.”

And we all laugh again.

I have been laughed at for this for more years than I care to count. I have been advised, warned, gently discouraged, loudly discouraged, and once — memorably — described as a hazard to mankind by a qualified music teacher.

The singer in me has heard all of this and found it completely irrelevant.

Because I know something most people don’t. I know what it feels like to stand under stage lights with a thousand souls in the dark in front of you, and sing your own words into that silence.

It doesn’t matter what they thought. What matters is that for one night, the stray dog had a stage.

And he sang.

— Stray Dog

routes.title: The Four Skills That Will Define the Next Decade
routes.seoTitle: The Four Skills That Will Define the Next Decade – Life as Sakti

My son — buried under the weight of 12th Board examinations and competitive entrance tests — walked out of his room. He didn't look…
routes.html:
An 11 PM conversation with my son led me to something I hadn’t quite articulated before — the only toolkit that truly matters now.

It was 11 PM on a weeknight. My son — buried under the weight of 12th Board examinations and competitive entrance tests — walked out of his room. He didn’t look exhausted. He looked curious. He saw me reading and simply sat down beside me, and within minutes, we were deep in conversation: geopolitics, philosophy, the latest discoveries in science, a film he had watched.

These late-night exchanges are the best part of my day. No agenda, no performance — just a father and a son thinking out loud together. I often remember how I used to do the same with my own father, pulling him into conversation regardless of whether he was tired or busy, and how he always made space to answer. My daughter, a wonderful listener, absorbs everything quietly. My son turns everything into a dialogue. Both are gifts.

That night, the conversation drifted toward something I had been turning over in my mind for weeks: the question of what it actually takes to survive and thrive in the decade ahead. Not just in IT — though that’s the industry that occupies most of my waking hours — but in any profession, any life.

In the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna stands paralysed on the battlefield of Kurukshetra — not because he lacks skill, but because he cannot see clearly. The field is familiar; the enemies are his own kinsmen. What he needs is not a new weapon. He needs wisdom, clarity, and the courage to act from it.

We in the IT industry stand at a similar Kurukshetra today. AI is reshaping everything we thought we understood about our work. The old maps no longer match the territory. And unlike television serials — where you can miss a week and catch up easily — this is a high-speed film. One distraction, and you have lost the thread.

That night, I shared with my son the four skills I believe will separate those who thrive from those who merely survive. I want to share them with you too.

Skill One

Curiosity

Everything begins here. Not the passive curiosity of someone who occasionally reads an interesting article — but an active, restless, almost hungry curiosity. The kind that makes you stay up past midnight exploring a concept, that makes you ask a second and third question when a first answer almost satisfies you.

Think of how Feynman described his relationship with physics — not as a professional obligation, but as a lifelong love affair where every answer opened ten more questions. Or closer to home, think of any person you know who seems to always be ahead of the curve. They are rarely the most formally educated. They are almost always the most relentlessly curious.

“Curiosity is not a personality trait. It is a daily practice. You either feed it or you starve it.”

In the age of AI, the half-life of specific technical knowledge is shortening dramatically. A skill you mastered in 2022 may be automated by 2026. What cannot be automated is the drive to learn the next thing before you are forced to. Curiosity is the engine of perpetual relevance.

My son, preparing for some of the toughest examinations in the country, already understands this intuitively. He doesn’t study topics — he inhabits them, pulling threads until the whole picture emerges. That is the habit to cultivate, whatever your age, whatever your field.

Skill Two

Awareness

Years ago, I heard the actor R. Madhavan speak about what he considers the defining quality of truly sharp, successful people. His answer surprised the audience — it wasn’t ambition, talent, or discipline. It was situational awareness. The ability to read a room, a moment, a shifting landscape — before others even notice it has shifted.

Curiosity without awareness is like having a powerful engine with no steering. You may go very fast in entirely the wrong direction.

Awareness means knowing where the conversations that matter are happening — and joining them. It means reading widely, yes, but also choosing your sources carefully in an era of algorithmic noise. It means cultivating a circle of people who challenge and inform you, not just comfort you.

“The most important awareness is knowing what not to follow — which groups to leave, which voices to mute, which rabbit holes lead nowhere.”

I have found, personally, that Twitter — when curated ruthlessly — is one of the most potent real-time intelligence tools available. The same feed that can waste three hours can, if managed well, keep you updated on what the sharpest minds in your field are thinking and doing right now. The tool is neutral; the curation is everything.

Awareness also means inner awareness — knowing your own biases, your blind spots, your tendency to dismiss the unfamiliar. Self-knowledge is situational awareness turned inward.

Skill Three

Empathy

Every conversation about AI disruption eventually arrives at the same question: what can humans do that machines cannot? The answer, consistently, is this — we can genuinely care about another human being’s experience. We can sit with someone in uncertainty. We can read the unspoken grief in a colleague’s silence. We can inspire trust not through logic alone, but through presence.

Consider the most influential leaders you have encountered in your career. Technical brilliance may have put them in the room. But it was empathy — the ability to understand what their teams needed, what their clients feared, what their stakeholders truly wanted beneath the stated requirements — that kept them there and elevated them.

“In a world of accelerating automation, the person who makes others feel seen will always have a seat at the table.”

The Upanishads speak of Tat tvam asi — “That thou art.” The recognition of yourself in the other. Empathy, at its deepest, is not a technique. It is an orientation toward the world: the understanding that the person across from you carries a universe as complex as your own.

In practical terms: listen more than you speak. Ask how people are — and wait for the real answer. When you lead a team, remember that behind every deadline and deliverable is a human being navigating their own Kurukshetra.

Skill Four

Communication

I have saved what I believe is the most underestimated skill for last and perhaps the one where the gap between what is needed and what most professionals can deliver is widest.

You can be the most curious, most aware, most empathetic person in the organisation. If you cannot communicate that value in writing, in speech, in documentation, in the quiet craft of setting context — you will be overlooked. Not unfairly. Simply invisibly.

We have, over the last decade or so, quietly surrendered our communication skills. We stopped writing long-form. We replaced memos with bullets, paragraphs with emojis, nuance with a brevity that mistakes itself for clarity. Our documentation became sparse. Our presentations became slides stripped of narrative. We delegated the craft of language to templates and abbreviations.

“Your identity, in the professional world, is shaped almost entirely by how you communicate. Everything else is background.”

And now, with AI tools enabling everyone to generate text at scale, the bar for excellent communication has paradoxically risen. Because when anyone can produce passable prose, what distinguishes you is not the words — it is the thinking behind them. Clear writing is clear thinking made visible.

This includes the new skill of prompting — the art of communicating precisely with AI systems to get meaningful output. It is the same underlying discipline as all good communication: know what you want, understand your audience, provide context, be specific. The medium changes. The craft does not.

Write more. Document diligently. Speak with intention. Blog, even if no one reads it at first. The practice compounds. One year from now, the person who has been writing regularly will think and communicate in ways that simply were not available to them before they started.

That 11 PM conversation with my son ended, as these conversations often do, without a tidy conclusion. He went back to his room. I returned to my book. But somewhere in the exchange, something got clarified — both for him and for me.

The decade ahead will be defined not by the specific tools we master — those will change faster than we can track — but by the qualities we cultivate as thinking, feeling, communicating human beings. The four skills above are not new. Philosophers and teachers have pointed toward them for centuries. What is new is the urgency.

Arjuna, in the end, did not win at Kurukshetra because he had the best bow. He won because Krishna helped him see clearly, act with integrity, and engage fully — even in the middle of profound uncertainty.

That is still, I believe, the only game worth playing.

— Sakti Bagchi

I sat down expecting a film about music. I got something else entirely a film about hunger, about the distance between good and great, and about the…
routes.html:
Why “Good job” may be quietly killing the best in us — and what great work actually demands.

My son asked me to watch Whiplash last week. I sat down expecting a film about music. I got something else entirely a film about hunger, about the distance between good and great, and about the terrible price of comfort.

Much of the movie stayed with me. The sweat, the blood, the obsession. But one line settled into my mind like a stone dropping into still water, and it hasn’t left since.

“The two most dangerous words in the English language are: Good job.”

I turned it over and over. Was this cruelty dressed up as philosophy? Or was it the most honest thing someone had said about talent in years?

The more I sat with it, the more I knew. It was the latter.

We Did Not Grow Up on Encouragement

I grew up in a world that offered no such softness. There was no applause waiting at the end of mediocre effort. There was criticism. There was silence. There was the blunt weight of expectation, unsoftened by praise. It felt terrible most of the time.

But something happened for those of us who did not turn away. Something almost miraculous, in the way that all difficult things, when survived, become miraculous in hindsight. The resistance — the friction of being told it was not good enough became the very fuel. We fought for the standard. We earned the standard. And the standard, earned that way, became ours forever.

The ones who gave up were, perhaps, always going to give up. That is a harder truth than it sounds. Encouragement does not change what is inside a person. It only delays the revealing of it.

Today, encouragement has become the default. We celebrate the attempt before the result. We hand out rewards before expectations are even met. We are seeking relaxation before we have grown tired enough. We are reaching for reward before we have arrived anywhere worth rewarding.

And slowly, quietly — we become useless to ourselves.

The Invitation We Keep Refusing

This brings me to a poem I have returned to many times over the years. It was written by Oriah Mountain Dreamer, and it asks — with tremendous gentleness and tremendous demand — the only questions that actually matter.

Oriah Mountain Dreamer — The Invitation

It doesn’t interest me what you do for a living. I want to know what you ache for and if you dare to dream of meeting your heart’s longing.

It doesn’t interest me how old you are. I want to know if you will risk looking like a fool for love, for your dream, for the adventure of being alive.

I want to know if you can sit with pain, mine or your own, without moving to hide it, or fade it, or fix it.

I want to know if you can live with failure, yours and mine, and still stand at the edge of the lake and shout to the silver of the full moon, “Yes.”

I want to know if you can get up after the night of grief and despair, weary and bruised to the bone, and do what needs to be done to feed the children.

I want to know if you will stand in the centre of the fire with me and not shrink back.

I want to know what sustains you from the inside when all else falls away.

I want to know if you can be alone with yourself and if you truly like the company you keep in the empty moments.

Read it again. Notice what she does not ask. She does not ask about your credentials, your titles, your accolades, how many people clapped for you. She asks if you can bear the weight of being alive — the weight of longing, of failure, of sorrow, of the fire.

That is not an encouragement. That is an invitation into something far older and harder and more true.

We are entering an age that will not be soft. The world is becoming more ruthless, not less. The polished surface of nicety is wearing thin. What lies beneath — in every professional arena, in every creative endeavour, in every life — is something that can only be discovered through difficulty.

So perhaps it is time. Time to retrain the mind. Time to stop treating hardness as an obstacle and start treating it as the path. Time to understand that everything worth having in this life will be — must be — hard-earned.

Not because suffering is noble for its own sake. But because the version of yourself that comes through the fire is the only version capable of standing at the edge of the lake and shouting, freely and without doubt, “Yes.”

— Sakti Bagchi

routes.html:
On the most dangerous gift one man can offer another

There is a man sitting across from you. A friend at chai shop or Cafe. A direct report in a one‑to‑one. A client on the other end of a video call.

You can see, with the clarity that only an outside eye possesses, exactly where he is going wrong. The story he keeps repeating. The habit that is quietly poisoning his marriage. The leadership blind spot that is slowly eroding the trust of his team.

You hold this truth like a lantern in your hands. If you lift it, he might finally see what has been in the dark for years. If you lift it, you might also scorch his pride, crack the friendship, shake his confidence before he is ready.

What do you do with a truth that could either light his path or burn the bridge between you?

The Hagakure — that fierce, intimate manual written by the samurai Yamamoto Tsunetomo in the early 18th century — says: not yet.

“First judge well whether that person is of the disposition to receive it or not.”

These are not the words of a cautious man hedging his bets. This is the wisdom of someone who has watched a thousand well‑meaning truths shatter like porcelain on a stone floor — not because the truth was wrong, but because it arrived before the soil was ready.

What follows is less a set of tips than a way of being with people: a samurai‑inspired method for offering hard truths so that others can actually receive them, drink from them, and even one day thank you for the gift.

I. The Preparation of the Ground

The Hagakure teaches that before any opinion is offered, you must first become close to the man. Not superficially close — not the closeness of shared offices and forced pleasantries — but the deep closeness where he trusts your word, continuously, without reservation. You must earn the right to hold his attention when you speak of difficult things.

Think of a manager who has to tell a high‑performing team member that their impatience is driving others away. The conversation doesn’t begin in the performance review where the critique is finally spoken; it begins months earlier in the coffees shared, the late‑night Slack messages answered, the small promises kept. By the time the truth arrives, the relationship has become a vessel strong enough to carry its weight.

Then, you approach the subject from the direction of what he loves. You find what is dear to him, his pride, his values, his sense of who he is and you seek the best way to speak so that you are truly understood. A hammer and a scalpel can both cut, but only one heals.

To “approach from the side” often sounds like this: “I care a lot about your growth here — would it be alright if I shared something I see that might be getting in your way?” Or: “Because I value this friendship, I don’t want to stay silent about something that touches what matters most to you.” The truth steps into the room slowly, hand open, instead of kicking down the door.

II. The Timing of Truth

Even with all this preparation, the samurai text counsels us to judge the occasion. There is when you are ready to speak — full of insight, charged with urgency — and there is when they are ready to hear. These are rarely the same moment.

Is this a moment for a letter — where words can be chosen and re‑read and absorbed in solitude? Or is it the moment of leave‑taking, that brief sacred window when a man’s defenses are lowered and his heart is open? Is it a quiet walk after a tense meeting, or the pause after a long project ends and everyone finally exhales?

Think of the worst possible moment to offer hard feedback: correcting your partner’s tone in the middle of a late‑night argument in the kitchen, or telling a colleague their presentation skills are weak minutes before they go on stage. Technically, the feedback might be accurate. Practically, it cannot be heard; it lands as attack, not assistance.

When was the last time someone chose the wrong moment with you — on the drive home, in front of others, in a rushed hallway conversation — and you felt your body armor slide into place? When was the last time you did the same to someone else because the truth was burning your tongue and you wanted relief more than you wanted to serve?

III. The Genius of Oblique Honesty

Here is where the Hagakure reveals something almost miraculous. To help a man see his own fault without humiliating him, speak first of your own faults — similar ones, close enough in shape that they become a mirror. Let the truth occur to him on his own, like a light he believes he found himself.

“Praise his good points and use every device to encourage him, perhaps by talking about one’s own faults — but so that they will occur to him.”

Notice the difference:

Blunt: “You undermine your own team. No one trusts your commitments.”

Oblique, praise‑first: “Your team rallies behind you because you care so fiercely about the work. I’ve had a similar drive, and I’ve seen how, when I over‑promise and scramble, people stop trusting my word. May I share something I’ve noticed in how deadlines are communicated on your projects?”

Or in a friendship:

Blunt: “You’re always late. It’s disrespectful.”

Oblique: “One of the things I love about you is how present you are when we’re together. I’ve been realizing in my own life how being even fifteen minutes late can quietly signal ‘you don’t matter as much as my schedule.’ I don’t want that to creep into our friendship, so I wanted to name it between us.”

A coaching client once told me that the most important feedback he ever received began with praise for his discipline and loyalty. Only then did his mentor say, “I used to cling to control for those same reasons and it slowly strangled my team. Let me tell you how I learned to loosen my grip.” By the time the mentor’s story ended, the client could see his own pattern clearly, without being pushed. The lantern was on the table between them, not swinging in his face.

This is not manipulation. This is love in its most patient form. It is the act of placing a candle in a dark room rather than shining a searchlight into someone’s eyes.

IV. The Thirst That Receives

And if all of this is done with care — the closeness cultivated, the timing respected, the ego bypassed — then something extraordinary happens. The person across from you stops bracing and starts leaning forward. Their shoulders drop. Their eyes stop scanning the room for exits and return to the space between you. Their questions shift from defending the past to wondering about the future.

The Hagakure describes it with one of the most beautiful images in all of its pages:

“Have him receive it the way that a man would drink water when his throat is dry — and it will be an opinion that will correct faults.”

Not water forced down a reluctant throat. But water received by a man who is parched, who reaches for it, who feels it as relief. You can hear it in the way he says, “Tell me more,” instead of, “Yes, but—.” You can see it in the way he pauses, looks down, and lets the words sink in before answering. That is the only kind of truth that actually changes anything.

When someone is not yet thirsty, you will notice a different texture: eyes flicking to their phone, arms crossed tightly, a quick rush to justify every point, jokes that swerve away from anything tender. In those moments, pressing the lantern closer only blinds them.

Instead, you might ask gentle, coaching questions that invite readiness: “How do you feel things are going on your team, honestly?” “Is there anything you’ve been sensing might be getting in your way lately?” These questions do not pour water; they help the thirst surface, so that when the truth finally comes, it can be received as something longed for, not imposed.

V. The Ancient Echo

At the bottom of my notes from this passage, I had written in Sanskrit:

The Hagakure is a text from 18th‑century Japan. The Sanskrit tradition is far older. And yet both arrive at the same understanding: wisdom is not a commodity you broadcast. It is a relationship you tend. Truth spoken without trust is noise. Truth spoken in love, at the right moment, in the right form — that is transformation.

Seen through this lens, the “most dangerous gift” becomes a simple, demanding sequence. First, prepare the ground: become worthy of being heard. Second, honor the timing: do not mistake your urgency for their readiness. Third, practice oblique honesty: praise what is strong, offer yourself as mirror, and let the other man discover the shape of the truth. Finally, wait for thirst: speak in such a way, and at such a moment, that the truth is taken in like water by a dry throat.

The next time you are tempted to give someone an opinion — in a performance review, a difficult parenting moment, a fragile late‑night conversation — pause. Ask yourself not whether you are right, but whether they are ready. Whether you have earned it. Whether you are speaking from love or from the need to be seen as wise.

Then choose your moment, lift the lantern carefully, and offer one true thing to one real person. Watch, and see whether they turn away from the light — or reach for it as if they have been thirsty for a long time.

routes.title: Why Books Are the One Screen-Free Habit Your Nervous System Is Begging For
routes.seoTitle: Why Books Are the One Screen-Free Habit Your Nervous System Is Begging For – Life as Sakti
routes.description: Reading books can be likened to Pratyahara, as both involve withdrawing attention from external noise. While many struggle with reading, it offers unique benefits that enhance our physiological state, promoting relaxation and focus. Engaging with a book fosters not only mindfulness but builds inner infrastructure essential for navigating a complex world.
routes.html:
Can we compare reading books simmilar to Pratyahara (One of the eight limbs of Yoga)?

I meet people every day who confess, almost apologetically, that they are not readers.

Some say they fall asleep after a page. Others say they simply get bored. And honestly? I get it. I’ve been there too. The thickness of a book has a way of deciding your motivation level before you’ve even opened the cover. It sits on the nightstand like a silent accusation.

Here’s what I’ve noticed though. We don’t have an attention problem. We have a design problem.

Think about why we love reels. They’re over in 15 seconds. Web series are engineered in bite-sized episodes. Even a four-hour film like Dhurandhar holds people with lower attention spans in their seats because the filmmaker does the heavy lifting. The sound effects, the visual hooks, the pacing all of it is handed to you. You just have to show up.

A book is different. Brutally, beautifully different.

It gives you letters. That’s it. The visuals, the soundtrack, the emotional atmosphere you have to build all of that inside your own head. The author can write a gripping scene, but you have to conjure the fog, the footsteps, the tension in the room. That is not a flaw in the medium. That is the entire point. A book doesn’t just ask for your time. It asks for your presence. And in doing so, it quietly does something to your nervous system that no reel, no podcast, no show can replicate.

The Science Behind the Stillness

Reading isn’t just entertainment. It’s a physiological intervention.

When you settle into a book and your attention narrows to a single thread of words, something measurable begins to happen in your body. Ancient brain circuits — the same ones that evolved for sustained focus — begin to activate. Your heart rate slows. Your breathing evens out. The muscles you didn’t even realise were clenched begin to release.

What’s happening beneath the surface is a fundamental shift in your autonomic nervous system. Most of us spend our days in sympathetic dominance — the “fight-or-flight” mode that keeps us alert, reactive, and exhausted. Reading, when done with genuine absorption, gradually walks you away from that edge and into the parasympathetic state: “rest-and-digest.” The body stops bracing. It begins to recover.

And fiction does something even more remarkable. Reading about a character running through a forest activates your motor cortex — the same region that fires when you run. Reading about grief activates your brain’s empathy circuits as if the loss were your own. Neuroscientists call this “embodied reading.” The story doesn’t just entertain you. It becomes a low-stakes rehearsal for real life, quietly building neural pathways for experiences you haven’t yet lived.

How to Make Reading Work for You

Knowing the science is one thing. Building the habit is another. A few principles that actually help:

Mix your reading. Nonfiction sharpens your analytical networks and feeds your professional mind. But fiction is where the deepest stress relief lives — it fully disengages you from problem-solving mode in a way that nonfiction rarely does. You need both.

Time it strategically. Reading before bed isn’t just a cozy ritual. It lowers circulating stress hormones and nudges the parasympathetic system into gear, preparing the brain for sleep in a way that scrolling actively prevents.

Build a ritual around it. A consistent chair, a consistent time, a cup of something warm — these cues train your brain to shift states faster. Over time, the ritual itself begins to relax you before you’ve read a single word.

Follow curiosity, not obligation. The nervous system benefits of reading depend entirely on genuine absorption. If you are reading a book out of duty and finding your eyes sliding across the words without registering them, put it down. Pick up something that actually pulls you forward. A book you’re curious about is medicine. A book you’re forcing yourself through is just another task.

What Patanjali Knew Long Before the Neuroscientists

There is a concept in Patanjali’s Yoga Sutras called Pratyahara — the withdrawal of the senses. It is the fifth of the eight limbs of yoga, sitting precisely at the bridge between the outer practices and the inner work. In pratyahara, the yogi learns to pull their attention inward, away from the constant stimulation of the external world, so that the mind can begin to settle into itself.

I am not claiming that reading a novel is the same as a yogi’s meditative practice. But I do believe they share a profound family resemblance.

When you are truly absorbed in a book, you have, in a very real sense, withdrawn your senses from the noise of the world. The notifications lose their grip. The internal chatter quietens. Your attention, usually scattered across a dozen inputs, gathers itself around a single thread of meaning. The body follows. It always does.

In a VUCA world — volatile, uncertain, complex, ambiguous — this capacity to withdraw, to recollect yourself, is not a luxury. It is a leadership skill. The calmest people in the room are rarely the ones who have the fewest problems. They are the ones who have built the inner infrastructure to not be driven by every stimulus that arrives.

Books build that infrastructure. One page at a time. One evening at a time.

You don’t have to be a “reader” to start. You just have to be curious enough to pick up one book that interests you, and honest enough to put it down if it doesn’t.

The nervous system will do the rest.

Inspired by Anne-Laure Le Cunff’s article on Big Think: “How Reading Books Regulates Your Nervous System“
