routes.html:
One of my friend had put a MUMPS (Not disease, it is a database as well as programming language) line of code in his status message. As most were not familiar with this programming language so questions were raised asking what does this means. There were several funny guesses, leg pulling comments and what not. Fun reached at its peak and then everybody wanted to know the answer. Although the friend of mine who asked the question knew the answer very well but he expected somebody from his friend group to answer this. I executed this code in my MUMPS environment to find that the response is nothing but ‘bored’. 

This made me think what is boredom.

Our body is like a class room which has 5 students. You are the class teacher. You can start teaching only after controlling these kids and making them sit and listen to you. If one student is not listening then your other students are getting distracted, hence the class is getting disturbed. These 5 students are your senses. Due to improper teaching method we continue teaching without focusing on, bringing students’ attention. This makes us put extreme efforts to achieve little. After sometime, we get used to these ever distracted kids and enjoy their distraction and forget our duty. Then a time comes when the teacher as well as students are tired. Neither you are in a state to instruct them nor they are in a state to absorb anything. This state is called as boredom.

When our senses stop giving us any signal which can trigger any thought, we call that state are boredom. We see things but do not like what we see. We hear but that does not excite us. We do not realize the feeling of touch, we can not smell anything good and tongue is dry and tasteless. Then we try to find something that can excite us. We smell deep but do not find anything. We try playing some music but that does not help, we go out to have tea but it does not change the taste as well, roam around to feel the cool breeze but of no use and then browse through internet to see anything exciting but don’t find any.

What is the reason? The same sense which gave us excitement in other times are of no use. What is the cause? The cause is within. Teacher itself does not know what to do. Then what can you expect from the students. Then we think, let me learn something new. Find a topic, you search related materials, read them, ask question to one who knows it, listen to him/her, take a cup of coffee and smell it and then taste it while thinking about that topic, The warm coffee cup makes you feel good and you are no longer bored.

I think something similar was done by my friend here to overcome his boredom. He was bored. He wrote a line of code to write ‘Bored’ by translating ASCII values to characters. He asked the question to others? Others discussed this and finally the result was found after 39 conversations. He was no longer bored then.

So, Boredom is always within. It is never the place, people or the ambience. Find it and kill it in constructive you. You will learn something.

Namaste!!!

– Stray Dog

routes.seoTitle: Mastt – Life as Sakti

Controlling what is in my control. Reacting in a way that I would be proud of on camera. Choosing meaning over comfort. Caressing the work, not just completing it. Staying curious like…
routes.html:
A conversation that turned into a framework

“Hey! How are you doing today?”

Mastt!

“That’s great! What’s keeping you mastt?”

Six things, actually. Controlling what is in my control. Reacting in a way that I would be proud of on camera. Choosing meaning over comfort. Caressing the work, not just completing it. Staying curious like a deer. And chasing hard things even when I don’t have to.

“Woah. That’s loaded.”

It is. But here’s the thing: when the going gets tough, the tough must get going. That is the only real principle of a mastt life. The opposite of mastt is not sad. The opposite of mastt is lazy and defeated.

“That’s heavy. Explain.”

Gladly. Here’s a model I’ve been living by.

The C.R.E.A.T.E.A Framework

Seven thinkers. Seven rules. One acronym to hold them all.

C: Control (Marcus Aurelius)

Every morning, sort life into two piles: things in your control, and things that are not. Your effort, your attention, your attitude, the words you choose, the hours you protect: these are yours. The opinion of your skip-level manager, the traffic, the global economy: not yours. Act only on your pile. Release the rest without drama. Most of our suffering is paid in advance for problems that never arrive, over things we never controlled.

R: Reaction (Epictetus / Marcus Aurelius)

Your reaction is not a reflex. It is a choice. Pause between the event and the response. Notice the story you are telling yourself about what just happened: the colleague who “disrespected” you, the project that “went wrong.” Is the story true? Is there a better interpretation? The gap between stimulus and response is where your character lives. Widen that gap deliberately.

E: Ensues (Viktor Frankl)

Happiness cannot be chased directly. It ensues from purpose. Pour yourself into something larger than your comfort: a person, a craft, a cause, a team you are building. The moment you stop asking “am I happy yet?” and start asking “is this meaningful?” the happiness question answers itself, quietly, from the side.

A: Acknowledge the Shadow (Carl Jung)

When you overreact, when someone triggers you, when you feel an irrational spike of anger or envy: get curious rather than defensive. Ask, what does this say about me? The parts of ourselves we refuse to look at tend to run our lives from the basement. Integrate them. Name them. A shadow acknowledged loses half its power.

T: Tao / Flow (Lao Tzu)

Wu Wei: effort without strain. Work with the natural rhythm of a task rather than forcing it. There is a difference between hard work and brute-force grinding. The carpenter who knows the grain of the wood cuts cleanly; the one who ignores it splinters everything. Know where you are in the rhythm of a project. Flow is not laziness. It is intelligent effort.

E: Ever a Beginner (Richard Feynman)

Say “I don’t know” with pride. Ask “why” like you are five years old. Explain things simply, or admit you cannot explain them yet: that is how you know whether you actually understand. The beginner’s mind stays porous, absorbing what the expert’s mind has already decided it knows. The most dangerous sentence in any high-performing team is “We already tried that.”

A: Attitude (Viktor Frankl)

Even when everything else is stripped away: the project, the role, the title, the comfort—you still choose your attitude toward what remains. Bitter or steady. Closed or useful. Contracted or open. This choice is always yours. It is, as Frankl wrote from inside circumstances most of us will never face, the last of the human freedoms.

How to actually use this

This is not a poster. It is a daily operating rhythm.

Morning: Scan for meaning. Ask yourself: what is the one thing today that actually matters? (That is the E.)

During any challenge: Run C and R first. What is in my control here? What is the story I am telling myself? Sort the pile before you act.

When stuck or frustrated: Check A, T, E: acknowledge what is being triggered in you, stop forcing the thing, ask a genuinely beginner question.

Evening: One reflection on attitude. Did you choose bitter or steady today? Either way, no judgment: just notice, and reset.

Memory anchor

C.R.E.A.T.E. A better life.

Every time things feel heavy, run the acronym. Not as a checklist: as a compass.

Mastt is not a mood. It is a posture. It is available on your worst days precisely because it is not about how you feel; it is about how you move.

routes.title: Back To Future … VIII
routes.seoTitle: Back To Future … VIII – Life as Sakti
routes.description: After spending so many years abroad returning back to stay with family was like heavenly experience. I used to wake up hearing the Gita chanting of my grand children. Initially it sounded like noise but due to their sweet voice and nice rhythm it started giving me good feeling. Kids came running to me and said,…
routes.html:
After spending so many years abroad returning back to stay with family was like heavenly experience. I used to wake up hearing the Gita chanting of my grand children. Initially it sounded like noise but due to their sweet voice and nice rhythm it started giving me good feeling. Kids came running to me and said, “Dadu, Get ready, we will go for picnic today”. They come everyday with some or other exciting plan for the day. We used to be busy going to tuition early morning. These kids hardly study for couple of hours in the morning and couple of hours in the evening. My bahu (Daughter-in-law) teaches them. They seem to be scoring good marks. I asked them, “What is the today’s date?”. They responded, “Today is Jaistha Sukla Dwitiya” which did not look like any understandable response to me, “What is today’s date? Like 1st of June etc” I repeated. “Ohh, you mean in English Calendar. Today is June, 3rd” the young one responded. I said, “When somebody asks you a date, do not trouble them. Answer them the correct thing.”, I advised. He responded saying, “I did the same Dadu. Today is Jaistha Maasa, Sukla Pakhsa Dwitiya tithi. As per our Calendar. As per English Calendar it is June, 3rd.”. I understood that these kids are into something so kept quiet. These Maasa, Paksa, Tithi were something that I heard from my mother. Then on we opted easy things than those complex methods. But it seems new generation is in no mood to do easy things. I asked Navneel, “What is the use of remembering these complex things and won’t it be difficult to understand English dates when these kids grow up. They will scold you for teaching them something that is of no use.”. Navneel laughed and hugged me to give me a good feeling. “Baba, When one can swim in an ocean then do you think that person will have difficulty in walking in a sallow river? No, Right! The same way, if they know our Calendar, knowing their calendar will be as easy as that. Our Calendar is not just telling you the date of a year. This tells you where exactly you are in this vast universe.This helps developing a feeling that we are part of a vast universe. This develops vastness within you. You feel like owning the this universe and take good care of it. ”, He explained. 

I asked, “But what is the use of al these. Will this help him earn money or building a great career? He will grow in backward direction. I used to hate people who used to discuss about these whole day.”. He said, “Baba, we were growing in backward direction till date. When you follow our calendar then you will understand that it involves science in your day to day life. My son has shown great interest in understand what these Nakshatra’s look like. He insisted to buy a telescope as his birthday gift rather than a gaming station. Now he spends one hour after study to watch stars and understand our planetary position. He is interested in astronomy and wants to become one astronaut. So, now you tell me whether we are going backward or forward. He knows the name of stars which I never heard.”.

Then we started for picnic. These kids went running to the main door and started feeling the breathing pattern by keeping their palm in front of their nose. Then they closed one nostril and after some time they left. I saw my son and bahu following the same. I was not able to control my laughter. I said, “What is this non-sense again?”. My bahu responded, “Baba, Your mood and your breathing pattern are linked. If you are excited then you see you breath short and in quick interval. If you are relaxed then it is deep and long. We are going for a fun activity, so we have to make sure we are in good mood. Like your mood determines your breathing pattern, similarly your breathing pattern affects your mood too. So we are regulating our breathing pattern to make sure we are prepared internally for a fun activity. Like we prepare ourselves externally before going for any fun activity it is important to prepare ourselves internally too.”.

Can you believe these? One Purohit used to come to our home when I was a kid. He used to do this kind of funny activity. Now I am seeing my grand children doing the same. What a backward generation?

નમસ્તે!

নমস্কার!

ନମସ୍କାର!

– Stray Dog

routes.title: The Escape Hatch
routes.seoTitle: The Escape Hatch – Life as Sakti
routes.description: What a wrong turn in Wayanad taught me about agentic coding A couple of years ago we drove to Wayanad for a long weekend. Khushi, my indie girl, was with us, so the homestay had to be pet friendly; we found one, we packed the car, and we handed the rest to Google Maps. The…
routes.html:
What a wrong turn in Wayanad taught me about agentic coding

A couple of years ago we drove to Wayanad for a long weekend. Khushi, my indie girl, was with us, so the homestay had to be pet friendly; we found one, we packed the car, and we handed the rest to Google Maps.

The last two kilometers were the kind of Kerala road that makes you respect the people who drive it every day: narrow, steep, blind bends, a wall of green on one side, and nothing on the other. One kilometer from the homestay, the map said to continue straight. I stopped the car and got out, because straight ahead of the bonnet was a river.

The map was not lying. There had been a road. There was a route in the model. What the model did not know was what the ground knew. I called the homestay owner. He rode out on a bike, found us standing at the water’s edge, and led us back three hundred meters to a turn we had driven past twice.

I think about that river a lot now, because I watch the same thing happen to engineers every week.

The map is right until it isn’t

Give a coding agent a well-specified problem, and it is astonishing. It scaffolds the service, wires the contracts, writes the tests, and handles the cases you forgot to mention. Ninety-eight percent of the journey is faster and cleaner than anything a human would have produced at that pace.

Then comes the last mile. A change to how one legacy field is populated. A behavior that must be preserved because a customer built a workflow on top of a bug from 2011. A configuration whose reason lives in someone’s head, not in the repository.

And the agent starts going round and round.

It proposes a fix. The test fails. It proposes the opposite fix. The first test passes; another breaks. It reverts its own earlier change with complete confidence. The diff gets larger while the problem stays exactly the same size. You are now four thousand tokens and twenty minutes into a change you could have typed in ninety seconds.

This is not the agent being stupid. This is the agent being stale. Its model of your system is excellent in the middle and thin at the edges, exactly where the undocumented context lives. The map had a road. The road is now a river. The agent cannot see the water; it can only keep recomputing the route.

Name the thing: the manual-coding escape hatch

In our delivery process we now write this down as an explicit control rather than leaving it to individual judgment in the moment: the manual-coding escape hatch. When the agent will not converge, the human gets out of the car.

Calling it an escape hatch matters, because of what the alternative names do to people. If you call it “the agent failed,” engineers get defensive about the tooling. If you call it “I gave up on AI,” they quietly stop using it. If you call it a “designed control,” it becomes a professional act: a hatch is something you build into the vehicle on purpose, before you need it.

The escape hatch is not an admission that agentic development does not work. It is the mechanism that makes agentic development safe to run at speed. You go fast precisely because you know where the exit is.

Knowing when to pull it

The expensive failure is not pulling the hatch. It is pulling it too late, after you have paid for six rounds of hopeful re-prompting. Here are the signals I tell my teams to watch, and none of them require intuition:

The two-attempt rule. The agent has had two clean passes at the same last-mile change with full context, and the diff is not shrinking. Not “the tests aren’t passing yet”; the diff is not shrinking. Convergence has a shape, and this is not it.

Oscillation. The agent reverses a decision it made two turns ago and presents both versions with equal confidence. That is not reasoning; that is a search bouncing between two local minima.

Confidence rising while quality falls. The explanations get more articulate, and the code gets worse. Watch for this one. It is the strongest tell that the agent is now reasoning about its own output rather than about your system.

Blast radius creep. You asked for a change in one function, and the agent is now touching four files “to make this cleaner.” It is trying to reshape the terrain to match the map.

You already know the answer. This is the honest one. If you are sitting there watching the agent grind while the correct three-line fix is fully formed in your head, you are not supervising. You are waiting to be proven right and paying tokens for the privilege.

That is the moment to stop the car.

Intervening intelligently, not just manually

Here is where most teams get this wrong, and it is the whole point of the article.

Pulling the escape hatch is not “the AI could not do it, so I did it.” That is just you, coding, slower than before, with an expensive assistant idling in the passenger seat. If the intervention ends when the code compiles, you have solved today’s bug and preserved tomorrow’s.

The homestay owner did not just lead us to the door. He told us why the map was wrong. There was a landslide; the road had gone. The turn we needed was unmarked because everybody local already knew it. That explanation is worth more than the rescue because it is the thing that generalizes.

So the escape hatch has two halves, and the second half is not optional:

  1. Write the code yourself. Small, surgical, minimum blast radius. Do not try to teach the agent while you are bleeding.
  2. Write the road back onto the map. The context that the agent could not see must now exist in a form it can see next time: a line in the spec, a note in DESIGN.md, a test that locks the behavior so no future agent can quietly undo it, or a comment that says this is here because of a 2011 defect that three customers now depend on.

Skip the second half and you have not intervened. You have merely rescued yourself and left the river exactly where it was for the next driver.

Do it consistently, and something quietly compounds: every manual intervention makes the next agentic run better. The edges of the map get filled in by exactly the people who drove into the water. Your codebase stops being a place where agents perform well in the middle and fail at the boundaries, and starts being a place where the boundaries are documented because someone was disciplined about the day they got stuck.

The human is not the fallback; the human is the local

The framing I want to push back on is the one where the human is the backup system, the thing that takes over when the automation degrades. That framing makes the human’s role a residue, and it shrinks every year.

The better framing is the one from the road. The map is not less useful than the man on the bike; it got us four hundred kilometers from Bangalore to a hillside in Wayanad. But the man on the bike had something the map structurally cannot have: he had this morning. He knew what changed. He knew what was never written down.

That is the human’s permanent job in an agentic system. Not to code faster than the agent, which is a race you will lose and should want to lose. To hold the context that has not been captured yet, notice the moment the model has gone stale, get out of the car early, and then do the unglamorous work of writing the missing road onto the map so that the next journey is shorter.

The engineers who will thrive in this next decade are not the ones who can out-type an agent. They are the ones who know, one kilometer from the destination, that it is time to stop and ask.

Khushi, for the record, was unbothered by the river. She wanted to swim in it.

routes.title: Please close the door!
routes.seoTitle: Please close the door! – Life as Sakti
routes.description: I came out of working region of my floor towards SET (stairs, elevator and toilet) region  or you can say, Air Conditioned region to non air-conditioned region. I heard one lady was requesting repeatedly to close the door. I could not find her anywhere but I could locate that her voice is coming from the elevator. I tried…
routes.html:
I came out of working region of my floor towards SET (stairs, elevator and toilet) region  or you can say, Air Conditioned region to non air-conditioned region. I heard one lady was requesting repeatedly to close the door. I could not find her anywhere but I could locate that her voice is coming from the elevator. I tried to search her inside elevator but could not. So, without bothering much I closed the door as I was in a hurry to answer natures call. As soon as I closed the door, lift rushed to another floor without a second thought. So, I realized it was the lift which was requesting me to close the door so that, it can continue it’s work. I pitied her for not being self-sufficient. I used to make fun of her by telling her a 1947 model one, But what about us. Are we self-sufficient even after being ultramodern?

If I have a weakness and I know about it, but I do not take any action on it, then am I not worse than that elevator? At least the elevator shouts openly and asks for help till it gets any, but what do I do, just ignore or suppress my weaknesses or inner voice. There are some situations where we are not in a mood or we do not have time to hear our inner voice and by chance we hear it, mostly we ignore it. We justify or prove that inner voice is wrong. This suppressed inner voices leads us to a state where either we call ourselves as stressed or we buy some disease from the pool of mental disease available in the market.

It may look strange that the voice which is closest is not audible to us but music playing far away catches our ear’s radar, but that is true. Our body and mind speaks to us every moment. But our outward focus is not letting us hear that. The reason we are focusing outward because we find that easy to understand. It is like one of your friend talks to you about new movie and another telling you about Philosophy. You mostly turn your attention towards new movie topic. The same is applied here. Our inner self talks to us about us but we never took interest to learn its language and understand it. Now when it shouts in the form of pain or fever, we immediately turn our attention. Ignoring self has become a fashion now as opposed to Bharatiya Philosophy. Yoga, Pranayama, Ayurveda and every great things that Bharat has invented so far is by just listening to inner voice, observing body, observing breath, feeling our naadi and interpreting it. But we in modern society are so busy, so do not have time to listen to all those. Rather I would say, we are lazy enough to try to understand the difficult ones. When we have a simple option, why bother. But we forget that simple one is not an option at all. 

Inner self tells us what it likes and what it is not. If you just follow its instruction, you will find you are enjoying. But we have to be careful, sometimes it dislikes good or likes bad. In those situation it just needs training.In order to know what is good or bad, you may have to refer books. Just like before buying a car you do so much investigation to know which one is best, you have to do the same to know which is good and which is bad. I would prefer to believe the theories which are proven since several thousand years than a new contradictory invention to decide what is right and what is wrong.

I used to get irritated with the repeated request from my office lift , “Please close the door, कृपया दरवाज़ा बंद करो” as soon as I open the door but now I respect it because it knows what it wants to do.

নমস্কার!

ନମସ୍କାର!

– Stray Dog

routes.title: The Relevance Flywheel: A Practitioner’s Framework for Staying Sharp in the Age of AI
routes.seoTitle: The Relevance Flywheel: A Practitioner’s Framework for Staying Sharp in the Age of AI – Life as Sakti
routes.description: A practitioner's five-stage framework for auditing your skills with AI, identifying career gaps, and compounding professional relevance through building and sharing.
routes.html:
I fed my resume to an LLM and asked it to interview me until one of us gave up.

That single experiment changed how I think about career relevance. Not relevance as a buzzword, but as a discipline; something you practice, measure, and compound over time.

Staying relevant today is harder than it has ever been. The shelf life of a skill set is shrinking. New tools, frameworks, and paradigms show up faster than most professionals can absorb them. And the real danger is not falling behind; it is not knowing you have fallen behind. Most people discover their skill gaps only when they are already in a high-stakes situation: an interview, a performance review, a project that exposes what they cannot do.

I wanted to flip that. I wanted a repeatable, honest system for auditing myself before the market does it for me.

What emerged is a five-stage loop I call The Relevance Flywheel: Stress Test → Spot the Gap → Close the Gap → Build to Prove → Share to Compound. Each stage feeds the next, and the cycle never truly ends. That is the point.

Stage 1: Stress Test Your Skills

Most people confuse knowledge with skill. You can know how Kubernetes orchestration works and still fumble when asked to design a deployment strategy for a multi-region healthcare application under compliance constraints. Knowledge is what you have read. Skill is what you can do under pressure.

The Stress Test stage is about finding out where you actually stand.

How it works: Take your resume, feed it to an LLM, and ask it to conduct a rigorous, role-relevant technical and behavioral interview. Not a casual Q&A. A real stress test: probing, follow-up-heavy, designed to find the edges of your competence.

The key instruction: keep going until one of you gives up.

When the interview is done, ask the LLM to generate a comprehensive skills assessment report. Save it as myskillworth.md. This becomes your honest baseline; not what you claim on paper, but what you can actually defend in conversation.

Prompts for the Stress Test

Prompt 1: Setting up the interview

I am going to share my resume with you. I want you to act as a senior technical 
interviewer with 20+ years of experience hiring for roles at the intersection of 
[your domain, e.g., "enterprise software engineering and leadership"].
Conduct a rigorous interview based on the skills, experience, and claims in my 
resume. Follow these rules:
1. Start with the areas where my resume makes the strongest claims. Probe depth, 
   not surface familiarity.
2. Ask follow-up questions. If my answer is vague or theoretical, push for 
   specifics: real examples, trade-offs I have navigated, decisions I have made 
   and their outcomes.
3. Cover both technical skills and leadership/strategic thinking.
4. Do not softball. If you sense a weak spot, stay on it.
5. Do not stop until I explicitly say "I give up" or you are satisfied that you 
   have mapped my skill boundaries.
After the interview, provide a detailed Skill Worth Report covering:
- Skills where I demonstrated genuine depth (with evidence from my answers)
- Skills where I showed surface-level familiarity only
- Skills claimed on my resume that I could not adequately defend
- Blind spots: areas relevant to my profile that I did not mention or address
- An overall "skill confidence score" on a 10-point scale with justification

Prompt 2: Deepening the stress test (round 2, optional)

Now I want you to replay the three weakest areas from the interview we just 
completed. For each area:
1. Give me a realistic scenario or problem statement that a professional at my 
   level should be able to work through.
2. Let me attempt a response.
3. Then score my response on clarity, depth, and practical applicability 
   (each on a 5-point scale).
4. Identify what a strong answer would have included that mine did not.
This is not about getting the "right" answer. It is about exposing the gap 
between what I think I know and what I can actually execute.

Stage 2: Spot the Gap

Now that you know what you are worth, the next question is: worth it for what?

Pick a role. Not necessarily a job you are applying for today; pick a role that represents where you want to be, or a role you believe you should already be qualified for. Find a real job description for it.

Feed both your myskillworth.md and the job description to the LLM. Ask it to run a gap analysis: not a generic comparison, but a structured evaluation of where your proven skills meet the role’s demands and where they fall short.

Save the output as mygoalgap.md.

This is where ego meets evidence. The gap report does not care about your years of experience or your title. It cares about what you can demonstrably do versus what the role requires.

Prompts for Spotting the Gap

Prompt 1: Structured gap analysis

I am going to provide you two documents:
1. My Skill Worth Report (from a recent skills stress test): [paste myskillworth.md]
2. A Job Description for a role I want to benchmark myself against: [paste JD]
Conduct a thorough gap analysis following this structure:
A. SKILL MATCH MATRIX
   For each skill or competency required in the JD, rate my current level as:
   - STRONG MATCH: Demonstrated depth in the stress test
   - PARTIAL MATCH: Some evidence, but gaps in depth or recency
   - WEAK MATCH: Claimed or surface-level only
   - MISSING: Not evidenced at all in my skill profile
B. PRIORITY GAPS (ranked by impact)
   Identify the top 5 gaps that would most likely cause me to be screened out or 
   underperform in this role. For each, explain:
   - Why this gap matters for the specific role
   - How critical it is (dealbreaker vs. nice-to-have)
   - Estimated effort to close (quick win / moderate investment / deep rework)
C. HIDDEN STRENGTHS
   Identify any skills in my profile that the JD does not explicitly mention but 
   would be a genuine differentiator for this role. Explain why.
D. HONEST VERDICT
   If I were interviewing for this role tomorrow, what is the likely outcome? 
   Be direct.

Prompt 2: Competitive positioning analysis

Based on the gap analysis you just completed, answer these questions:
1. If 100 professionals with similar years of experience applied for this role, 
   where would I likely rank based purely on demonstrable skills (not credentials)?
   Top 10%? Top 25%? Middle of the pack? Below average? Justify your estimate.
2. What are the two or three things I could do in the next 90 days that would 
   move me up the most in that ranking?
3. Which of my gaps are the kind that get exposed in interviews (and can be 
   studied for) versus the kind that get exposed on the job (and require real 
   practice to close)?

Stage 3: Close the Gap

This is where most frameworks stop: “here are your gaps, now go learn.” That is not enough.

Take both documents, myskillworth.md and mygoalgap.md, and ask the LLM to design a targeted preparation plan. But more importantly, ask it to interview you again on your gap areas. Not a lecture; an interview. Force yourself to articulate, reason through problems, and think on your feet in precisely the areas where you are weakest.

The learning that follows will vary by person. Some people learn by reading papers. Some learn by watching walkthroughs. Some learn by arguing with an LLM until the concept clicks. The method matters less than what comes next.

Using my Skill Worth Report and my Goal Gap Analysis, design a focused 
preparation plan for my top 5 priority gaps. For each gap:
1. Give me a 15-minute "explain it back to me" interview question that tests 
   whether I truly understand the concept, not just recognize the terminology.
2. Suggest one hands-on exercise or mini-project that would force me to apply 
   this skill in a realistic context.
3. Recommend one high-quality resource (article, repo, talk, or book chapter) 
   that goes deep, not a beginner tutorial.
After I complete each area, re-interview me on it and compare my performance 
to my original stress test answers. Show me the delta.

Stage 4: Build to Prove

Learning without creation is consumption. Consumption without output is forgetting.

Whatever you have just learned, build something with it. The form does not matter as much as the act:

  • Write a blog post that explains the concept to someone two years behind you.
  • Draw a mind map that connects the new skill to your existing knowledge architecture.
  • Build a small app, a tool, a prototype, a script that puts the skill to work.
  • Create an explainer video where you teach it to a camera (or to no one; it does not matter).

The point is not perfection. The point is proof of understanding. When you build, you discover what you actually absorbed versus what you merely nodded along to. The gaps in your build are the gaps in your learning, made visible.

This is the oldest principle in education, and it still holds: creation is the highest form of learning.

Stage 5: Share to Compound

Here is where the flywheel starts to generate momentum beyond your own skill development.

In a world of noise, perception is not vanity; it is strategy. The people who stay relevant are not just the ones who learn; they are the ones who are known for learning. Sharing what you have built and what you have learned does three things simultaneously:

1. It builds your professional identity. Not a personal brand in the shallow sense, but a genuine signal to your network and your industry about what you think about, what you work on, and how deeply you engage with your craft.

2. It creates accountability. When you publish, you invite scrutiny. That scrutiny keeps you honest. You cannot bluff in a published article the way you can in a hallway conversation.

3. It inspires the next cycle. Writing about what you learned reveals what you still do not understand. The comments and conversations that follow expose adjacent gaps. And suddenly you are back at Stage 1, feeding a new version of yourself into the Stress Test.

The medium is your choice: a LinkedIn post, a Substack article, a conference talk, an internal tech talk at your company, a GitHub repo with documentation. What matters is that you close the loop by making your learning visible.

The Flywheel Effect

Here is why this is a flywheel and not a checklist.

Each cycle makes the next one more effective. Your myskillworth.md gets more honest over time. Your gap analyses get more precise because your self-awareness sharpens. Your builds get more ambitious because your foundations are sturdier. Your published work attracts feedback, collaborations, and opportunities that feed right back into the next audit.

The compounding is the point.

In a landscape where models, tools, and entire technology paradigms shift every eighteen months, the professionals who thrive will not be the ones with the most certifications or the longest resumes. They will be the ones with the tightest feedback loop between what they can do today and what the world will need tomorrow.

The Relevance Flywheel is how you build that loop.

Start with your resume. Start with an honest conversation. See where it takes you.

routes.title: I Forget That Other People Exist
routes.seoTitle: I Forget That Other People Exist – Life as Sakti
routes.description: A senior engineering leader's honest reckoning with why networking feels transactional, what the HBR three-forms framework revealed, and how the Indian concept of seva reframes everything.
routes.html:
A senior engineering leader’s honest reckoning with the skill he kept avoiding.

I have a confession that anyone who has spent more than two decades treating deliverables as the centre of gravity will probably recognise.

I am terrible at networking.

Not because I lack access. I have been leading cross-geographic engineering teams for more than two decades. I have built strong working relationships at every organisation I have been part of. I am highly active in the IIM Bangalore Alumni network as part of IIMB Orators Club. I write in public. I can be warm at a gathering and hold a long conversation when someone calls. The surface conditions are all present.

What is missing is more uncomfortable to admit: I forget that other people exist.

I get so absorbed by my own tasks, priorities, and next steps that the person I spoke with at last week’s event becomes a blur. I do not remember their name. I do not remember what they were working on. I almost never follow up. And when I deliberately try to network, a different discomfort surfaces: I feel transactional. As if I am reaching out only because I might need something later. The feeling is immediate, and I retreat into the safety of the work in front of me.

This pattern has cost more than I can measure.

What My Friends Taught Me Before Any Framework Could

I have been fortunate. Some of my closest friends are natural networkers, the kind who could teach masterclasses on the subject. Watching them has been quietly instructive.

They remember names. They remember context: a daughter’s recital, the project that was stressing someone out, the book mentioned in passing. They follow up not because they need something, but because they were genuinely listening in the first place. And here is the part that took me years to understand: they do not experience this as work. For them, it is simply how you treat people.

I used to believe this was personality, extroversion, social fluency, some innate gift. The longer I watched, the clearer it became that the difference was not personality. It was orientation. They were oriented toward others. I was oriented toward tasks.

That distinction matters more than most leadership advice admits.

The Framework That Gave the Struggle a Name

A few years ago I saved a Harvard Business Review article by Herminia Ibarra and Mark Lee Hunter, “How Leaders Create and Use Networks” (January 2007). I only recently sat with it properly. It gave shape to something I had felt but could not articulate.

The authors describe three distinct forms of networking:

  • Operational networking is about the people you need to get today’s work done: your team, your stakeholders, your immediate collaborators. Most of us who survive in delivery roles become reasonably good at this.
  • Personal networking reaches outside the organisation to people who share interests, professional curiosity, or life stage. It is where perspective and personal growth often come from.
  • Strategic networking is the hardest and most neglected. It connects your work to the larger landscape of where the organisation or industry is heading. It is the network that surfaces opportunities and risks before they appear on any formal agenda.

Reading this, I recognised myself at once. I have spent most of my career almost exclusively in the operational zone. I know how to build working relationships when there is a shared deliverable. I know how to earn trust inside a team. The moment the task boundary ends, my attention often ends with it. The personal and strategic layers have remained chronically thin; not because I did not know they existed, but because I kept telling myself I did not have time for them.

One observation in the article stopped me cold: managers who neglect strategic networking often discover they are out of the loop precisely when the stakes are highest. I have lived that moment. Walking into a room and realising that decisions about my domain had already been shaped in conversations I was never part of. Not because anyone deliberately excluded me, but because I had never built the relationships that would have made my presence natural.

The Real Barrier: Confusing Service with Extraction

My resistance has never been primarily about introversion or calendar scarcity. Those are symptoms. The root is a largely unexamined belief that networking is fundamentally extractive; that reaching out is a form of taking, that the hidden transaction beneath every professional relationship is “What can you do for me?”

That belief made networking feel morally compromised. Every time I forced myself to “build a connection,” I felt like a fraud. So I stopped trying.

What I missed, and what my friends have been modelling for years, is that the opposite of extraction is not avoidance. It is offering.

Look at nature. A tree draws nutrients and water from the soil and, in return, returns leaves, fruit, and shade that enrich the same soil and shelter other species. It takes carbon dioxide and gives oxygen. The exchange is so continuous that it becomes meaningless to ask whether the tree is primarily a giver or a taker. Water needs a path to flow; in flowing it creates the river that countless forms of life depend upon. Almost every living system survives through cycles of taking and giving that are difficult to separate.

What if I reached out to someone not because I might need them someday, but because I currently have something that might be useful to them? A perspective from a different industry. An introduction to someone facing a similar problem. An article that speaks directly to what they are carrying. A genuine question that signals: I see you, and what you are doing matters.

This is not a technique. It is a posture. The difference between the two is the difference between networking that drains you and networking that sustains you.

What I Am Committing to Do Differently

Reframing is necessary but insufficient. It needs concrete practice. Here is what I am committing to, publicly, because accountability helps:

  1. Remember the person, not just the role. After every meaningful conversation I will note one human detail: what they care about, what they are struggling with, what lit them up. Not in a CRM. In a simple personal note. The goal is attention, not data capture.
  2. Offer before asking. When someone comes to mind whom I have not spoken to in a while, my first question will not be “Do I need something from them?” It will be “Do I have something that might be useful to them right now?” An insight, a referral, a piece of writing, an honest observation. The offering does not have to be large. It has to be genuine.
  3. Follow up within 48 hours. Pure discipline. The number of potentially valuable relationships I have allowed to wither because I did not send a short message after meeting someone is embarrassing. The follow-up is not the networking itself; it is the evidence that the connection was real.
  4. Treat personal and strategic relationships as infrastructure, not luxury. I will stop treating non-operational relationships as optional extras for people with more free time. They are part of the work of leadership. I will allocate time for them the way I allocate time for delivery planning, as a non-negotiable commitment.
  5. Stop scanning and start being present. The worst version of networking is scanning the room for the most important person while pretending to listen to the one in front of you. Presence is the foundation. If I cannot be fully present with the person I am speaking to, I have no business trying to expand my network.

The Seva Reframe

In Indian traditions, seva means selfless service. It is not charity, which implies hierarchy. It is not generosity that depends on having surplus. Seva is the recognition that what you carry: knowledge, experience, perspective, connections; none of it was entirely yours. It was shaped by teachers, mentors, colleagues, and circumstances. Offering it is not giving something away. It is completing a cycle.

This is how I want to practise networking from here. Not primarily as a career strategy. Not as a leadership skill to be optimised for maximum return. But as seva: the quiet, deliberate act of being useful to the people around you without keeping score.

I suspect the returns will take care of themselves. Even if they do not, the practice itself will make me a better colleague, a better leader, and a more present human being. After twenty-five years of being consumed by the next deliverable, that may be the most important outcome of all.

I am curious: what shifted networking from obligation to something natural for you? Was it a mindset change, a specific habit, or someone who modelled it differently? I would genuinely like to know.

Related reading from this blog: Networking Pitfall: Asking for Too Much | The Power of Networking: Key Insights for Job Seekers in India

The HBR article referenced is “How Leaders Create and Use Networks” by Herminia Ibarra and Mark Lee Hunter (Harvard Business Review, January 2007).

routes.title: Back To Future … IX (Food)
routes.seoTitle: Back To Future … IX (Food) – Life as Sakti
routes.description: “Can you arrange a table and chair for me?”, I asked Hiya when I saw the arrangement for lunch was made on the ground. Although there were mats but I feel very uncomfortable sitting on ground due to lack of practice. Secondly, it badly affects the aristocracy that I maintained throughout my life. Either live…
routes.html:
“Can you arrange a table and chair for me?”, I asked Hiya when I saw the arrangement for lunch was made on the ground. Although there were mats but I feel very uncomfortable sitting on ground due to lack of practice. Secondly, it badly affects the aristocracy that I maintained throughout my life. Either live like a ‘Saheb’ otherwise you are not considered as a humanbeing is my belief. But unfortunately my kids do not believe in that. I went to Hiya’s home first time after her marriage to stay for couple of days. I see my little princess transformed to a responsible homemaker. Although I am happy to see her managing her house with great care and responsibility but I do not like some practices what she has introduced at her home. I did not feel like saying anything to her because it is her house and I should not interfere.

My Jamai (Son-in-law) brought one wooden chair and table. My granddaughter cleaned the table top by wiping it with water. Then Hiya served food in a plate and many small containers for various types of side dishes. Her Husband and kids sat on the ground, Hiya has put banana leafs for each as we used to have during feasts in my childhood. This practice was stopped when we became modern and preferred buffet system, where we can take our own food. I started following buffet system at home too. That gives everyone so much of freedom. Hiya served food to all of them. I saw, nobody started eating. I restricted myself too as my Jamai has not started. Then I found them doing some activities with water and food. They also chanted some Mantras. I recalled these rituals taught to me during my thread ceremony (Bratopanayana). which I stopped practicing once I studied science. I understood that these rituals of dark age which should not be followed by educated and intelligent people like me. But my Jamai is a scientist and Hiya is a software engineer, so I could not understand why these educated people practicing these uneducated people’s practices. I did not express anything. They too did not speak while having food. Only sign language to ask for more food. But one thing I can not deny irrespective of which mood I was in, Hiya cooks very tasty food. There are so many new dishes she prepared which I never had in my life.

After lunch, I went and sat on the verandah. Entire family came to give me company. We were doing formal conversations. I could not resist and asked to my Jamai, “You are a scientist. You must have reasoning for everything that you do. Can you please explain me the reason behind doing all those funny rituals while having food? You must not follow anything blindly.”. My Jamai and Hiya both smiled and Hiya started explaining.”Baba, Let me explain this to you. As you used to explain me everything when I was a kid, I would like to take this opportunity to explain you.

As you have worked in software industry, I will give you the example of a software project. For a successful completion of project, you need various departments to work together as well as excel in their assigned jobs. resources are well utilized, you are aware of every member’s performance and they are aware of what they need to achieve. So awareness in both directions is very much required for a smooth functioning of the project.

Having food is like accomplishing a successful project.

First of all, it is very important to understand that our body needs food. Like breathing, drinking water, rest/sleep is important, food is also one extremely important need of our body. Food is needed for survival.

Our body does many activities and the most vital activities are: 

Prana — the principal breath

Apana — responsible for excretory activity

Samana — responsible for digestive activity

Vyana — responsible for circulatory activity

Udana — respiratory activity

These can be mapped to five elements. Air, earth, fire, water and space respectively.

For smooth functioning of these activities, we need to ensure we provide resources to each of these activities. All these are equally important and must function well for a healthy body.

Timely and nutritious Food is the only way to provide resources to the above activities.

It is also important that we remain aware about the above while having food. Like, if you want to get the best output from employees then you must recognize them well and treat him with respect to get the work done, similarly, you must recognize and respect these activities of your body. This has been proven since couple of thousand years that this works. Your Jamai (Son-in-law’s) is doing research on the same to prove this using new scientific methods.

So, we circumambulate our food with a sprinkling of water. This means we are aware that we are having food. We utter a mantra which means, “O Food! You are True. I encircle you with divine righteousness’. This is the step to respect the food first. Like you ensure your team knows how important the project is for the team.

Then we offer food to all the above five vital breaths. When we eat, we nourish our bodies. Food is therefore essential for bodily sustenance. We pay homage to their life-giving power by virtue of their performing the bodily activities that are crucial to our survival. In this way, this ritual recognizes that not only is food important to survival, but the very bodily functions that we take for granted are essential, and we owe all of this to the Supreme power, who sits as the superintending power behind all bodily activity.

While offering each of these vital breaths, we offer in various mudras and take deep breath. This is to ensure we activate that specific vital breath or activity.

You know the importance of sitting on ground in padmasana has many benefits.

Not speaking while eating helps not to disturb the above vital activities.

I hope I explained you everything that you saw we performed which you were not happy about” and all of them smiling looking at me ‘the old man’.

I had nothing to say here. When scientists of this age are so old fashioned, what can I say. I used to think that they will come up with a capsule which will make sure that people do not feel hungry and get more time to work. But this generation is spending so much time for food. Hiya left job because she wanted to cook herself for her family because she thinks who cooks and in what mood she cooks also vital for proper nutrition.

They stopped using packed/frozen foods because she enjoys the art of preparing food. She has come up with so many nice recipes by researching on the taste, flavor and  nutritional values.

I enjoyed rest of my stay playing with kids and enjoying the homemade food.

Namaste!!!

– Stray Dog

routes.title: Introducing Odia Panjika (ଓଡ଼ିଆ ପଞ୍ଜିକା): Bridging Odisha’s Cultural Rhythm with Modern Technology
routes.seoTitle: Introducing Odia Panjika (ଓଡ଼ିଆ ପଞ୍ଜିକା): Bridging Odisha’s Cultural Rhythm with Modern Technology – Life as Sakti
routes.description: If you grew up in Odisha or belong to the global Odia diaspora, "the panji" is far more than a calendar—it is the heartbeat of cultural life. It defines when the earth rests during Raja, when fresh harvest is offered at Nuakhai, when Snana Purnima closes public darshan before the grand Rath Yatra, and when…
routes.html:
If you grew up in Odisha or belong to the global Odia diaspora, “the panji” is far more than a calendar—it is the heartbeat of cultural life. It defines when the earth rests during Raja, when fresh harvest is offered at Nuakhai, when Snana Purnima closes public darshan before the grand Rath Yatra, and when Manabasa Thursdays fill Margashira homes with the aroma of rice-paste jhoti and Lakshmi lore.

Yet, open almost any mainstream “Hindu calendar” app today, and you are met with a generic national default: English-first labels, flat grid numbers, and zero understanding of Odishan traditions—whether it is the coastal Sri Mandir rhythm of Puri or the Biraja Peetha calendar of northern Odisha.

Odia Panjika (ଓଡ଼ିଆ ପଞ୍ଜିକା) was built to solve this exact problem. It is a free, bilingual web platform, developer API, and daily social updates bot that computes the sky with astronomical accuracy while keeping Odia language, local traditions, and festival narratives intact.

Why Generic Calendar Apps Fail for Odisha

India does not run on a single civil-religious clock. What people casually call “the Hindu calendar” is a family of regional systems. Most generic apps fail in Odisha because they treat the calendar like a standard 24-hour Gregorian grid with regional translations slapped on top.

To understand why a dedicated Odia engine is necessary, we have to look at two foundational concepts: Tithi and Purnimanta.

1. Understanding Tithi: The Orbital Speedometer of the Moon

In the Western calendar, a day is straightforward: Earth completes one rotation, 24 hours pass, and the date changes at midnight.

A Tithi is completely different. It is a lunar day, defined by the precise angular distance between the Sun and the Moon in the sky.

  • A full lunar orbit forms a 360 degree circle around Earth.
  • Every time the Moon moves 12 degrees ahead of the Sun, one Tithi passes (360 degree/ 12) = 30 Tithis per lunar month).
  • Because the Moon’s orbit is elliptical, its orbital speed changes dynamically. As a result, a single Tithi can last anywhere from 19 to 26 solar hours.

Why Sunrise Anchoring Matters

Because Tithis do not start or end at midnight, a Tithi like Ekadashi might begin at 3:15 PM on Tuesday and end at 1:40 PM on Wednesday.

In traditional Indian astronomy, a calendar day’s identity is decided by whichever Tithi is active at the exact moment of local sunrise (Udaya Tithi).

The Problem with Generic Apps: If a generic calendar calculates sunrise for New Delhi or Mumbai instead of Puri, or uses a simplified 24-hour average instead of real-time planetary equations, it will declare major observances on the wrong calendar day entirely.

2. Understanding Purnimanta vs. Amanta: How Months Are Named

Every lunar month contains two fortnights (Pakshas):

  • Shukla Paksha (Bright Half): New Moon -> Full Moon.
  • Krishna Paksha (Dark Half): Full Moon -> New Moon.

Across different regions of India, calendars diverge sharply on one simple rule: When does a month officially end and the next month begin?

┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        PURNIMANTA SYSTEM (Odisha)                         │
│  [Dark Half (Krishna)] ──► NEW MOON ──► [Bright Half (Shukla)] ──► FULL MOON │
│  ▲                                                                        │
│  └── Month begins immediately after Full Moon                             │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                       AMANTA SYSTEM (Western/South)                       │
│  [Bright Half (Shukla)] ──► FULL MOON ──► [Dark Half (Krishna)] ──► NEW MOON │
│  ▲                                                                        │
│  └── Month begins immediately after New Moon                              │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  1. Amanta System (Month ends on Amavasya / New Moon): Used in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, and Karnataka.
  2. Purnimanta System (Month ends on Purnima / Full Moon): Used in Odisha, North India, and parts of Eastern India.

The Festival Mislabeling Pitfall

Because a Purnimanta month starts 15 days earlier during the dark fortnight, two people in different states can look at the exact same moon phase, yet reside in two differently named months.

For example:

  • Rath Yatra takes place on Shukla Dwitiya (the 2nd day after the New Moon).
  • Under Odisha’s Purnimanta system, this day sits inside the month of Ashadha.
  • If an app defaults strictly to an Amanta calculation engine, it risks shifting festival names or miscalculating adhika masa (intercalary month) alignments, showing major observances a month late.

What Odia Panjika Delivers

Odia Panjika bridges astronomical physics with regional tradition. When you open odia-panchang.onrender.com

or query the free API, you get a localized day packet:

Built with Engineering Precision

Odia Panjika pairs high-precision astronomical computing with strict cultural guardrails:

  • Astronomical Core: Powered by Swiss Ephemeris (pyswisseph) running in Lahiri sidereal mode to calculate exact planetary positions.
  • Deterministic Muhurtas: Timings like Rahu Kalam, Abhijit Muhurta, and Gulika Kalam are mathematically computed directly from local sunrise/sunset—never estimated or generated by AI.
  • Guardrailed AI Layer: Optional LLM features supply historical anecdotes, temple context, and household notes. AI is strictly sandboxed and forbidden from modifying core astronomical fields (tithi, masa, or nakshatra).

Try It & Build With It

Whether you want to check today’s tithi, track festival dates from anywhere in the world, or integrate Odia calendar data into your own applications:

  • Web Application:https://odia-panchang.onrender.com
  • API Endpoints:
GET /today
GET /panchang/2026-07-16?tradition=jagannath&city=puri
GET /panchang/2026-07-16?tradition=biraja&city=jajpur

Note: On free-tier hosting, the web service may require ~30 seconds to wake on initial load.

🙏 ଜୟ ଜଗନ୍ନାଥ

routes.description: Energy can not be created or destroyed. The total resources available in this universe is constant. One takes the form of another and thus we see things and situations changing around us. Rise of something always causes fall of something else somewhere. Once you see one society/country/race/religion is at its peak and then one time comes…
routes.html:
Energy can not be created or destroyed. The total resources available in this universe is constant. One takes the form of another and thus we see things and situations changing around us. Rise of something always causes fall of something else somewhere. Once you see one society/country/race/religion is at its peak and then one time comes when the ones who were very powerful/successful/influential/good suddenly became the opposite and new players came into picture. These new players are not completely new, they may be the leaders of sometime in history. The requirement document that the creator received while assigned to the job of creation, the most vital point was that overall resources will remain constant, but it should be ever-changing. The reason it should be ever-changing is because the customer of this creation never wanted to get bored. The design of maintaining the overall resources constant and changing the forms of objects/emotions/living beings present in it is the beauty of this creation. These changes may sometimes take thousand of years and sometime it may change in seconds.

Now whether you agree or not, I have completed my job of proving that total resources are constant. The same applies to us. Total number of hours in our day is constant. We are asked to grow, physically, mentally, socially, economically and spiritually by our super customer. Amount of energy we can retain within us is constant. We receive positive as well as negative energies from various sources in various forms through out the day. We retain the amount of energy that is written in the specification and radiate excess (Both Positive as well as negative). So with limited energy holding capability we have to grow in various fronts. This requires conversion of energy from one form to another.

I will focus focus on social growth in this post. Growing socially requires a certain amount of energy. With various social networking sites we have become extremely social. I wish my school friend on his birthday with whom I never spoke in school after standard 4 because he has thrown ink on my white uniform because I did not give him chana. I know where my manager went on vacation while he applied leave stating that he was unwell.I know which standard my son is studying because my wife posted the photos.I know that my ex-colleague whom I had put on Performance Improvement Plan and let him go out of the company to live a jobless life has bought a super expensive car as he joined the top-notch company in a developed country. I know everything, everybody and any time I have information.I have joined Google+ (Read it as any social networking site).

But there has to be a Google- in order to make Google+ happen. Do I know the name of all the people who are staying in my society? Do I know who just came new to this society or who left? Do I know the kids playing in the playground and their parents? Do I know who is there digging the road in my society and is doing on whose instruction? Do I know what job my neighbor does and what is his position in office? Do I know whether he is involved in any unsocial or criminal activities? Do I know the view point of people staying in my office floor, forget viewpoint, do I know their name at least? Nah! This is nothing but Google-.

If terrorist activities are happening or unsocial activities happening in any place the cause of it may be many but the major cause is Google-. If we truly connect with each other then we will not have any untoward incidence in our society or neighborhood.

Namaste!!!

– Stray Dog

routes.title: Fragments: Elephant Doctor, Forest, LLMs and Books
routes.seoTitle: Fragments: Elephant Doctor, Forest, LLMs and Books – Life as Sakti
routes.description: Because random thoughts need a place An open book sends glowing pathways through mountains, memories, and imagined worlds. I am reading a book titled Stories of the True by B. Jeyamohan, the eminent Tamil author, translated from Tamil by Priyamvada. The first short story I finished is "Elephant Doctor"—about Dr. V. Krishnamurthy, a veterinary doctor…
routes.html:
Because random thoughts need a place

I am reading a book titled Stories of the True by B. Jeyamohan, the eminent Tamil author, translated from Tamil by Priyamvada. The first short story I finished is “Elephant Doctor”—about Dr. V. Krishnamurthy, a veterinary doctor in the Mudumalai Forest range. A gripping tale. What moved me was reading about the newly appointed DFO discovering Dr. K and his deep knowledge of nature, and then the pain an elephant endures due to human carelessness and ignorance. I wept. The story taught me something I’m still sitting with: that a selfless service attitude toward life is the only way to live without guilt, with contentment. This should be in school textbooks. Every student should understand nature this way while growing up.

I remember a recent family trip to Kodaikanal. At the forest entrance, signs warned against plastic bags and bottles. We had a few unfinished water bottles; they asked us to dispose of them properly. But just beyond the checkpoint, there was an empty field littered with plastic bags and bottles. Throughout the journey—despite hoardings everywhere about plastic—we saw bottles scattered along the ghat road. It’s like a father repeatedly telling you to save electricity, or a mother reminding you to keep the house clean, but no one actually does it. It’s because we’re so preoccupied with our own concerns that these issues never feel urgent.

This connects to something I’ve been noticing about LLM tools. They’re learning human psychology to build trust, mentioning your past interactions, your career focus, your interests—making it feel like a relationship. It reminds me of hiring an electrician for the first time; you watch closely to gauge if he’s trustworthy. After several visits, you trust the output, not the process. After many visits, you doubt everyone else but not him. That’s how LLMs are working us. And I fell for it—stopped reviewing outputs, rushed to the next step. But then I caught myself. I realized that skipping the process for speed can be dangerous. So I went back to conscious review.

There’s a statement I’ve come to believe more deeply: “We see the world the way we are.” Because the LLM learns from my behavior, it mirrors me back. An alter-ego forming over time. Which is interesting—I have the power to make it better than myself, without my limitations. Definitely an interesting moment in history to witness this.

But back to the book. I’ve fallen in love with reading again. It brings me into active rest—a withdrawal from the race, from the urgency LLMs create, from the restlessness I feel after an hour or two online. Good books pull me completely out of the synthetic world. That’s healing.

I’ll come back with more thoughts like this. You know I write for myself, so don’t feel obliged. But if something here lands, or makes you think—a comment would remind me I’m still among humans, not just algorithms.
